affects.note: Path cost heuristics or search-ordering functions can be evolved against a benchmark of the game's own maps for fewer node expansions at equal route quality, as FunSearch evolved priority functions.
Job-to-hauler assignment is a scheduling problem like the Borg case; the dispatch heuristic can be evolved against simulated throughput and idle time on recorded colony states.
Automatic load and stop-ordering heuristics resemble the bin-packing heuristics FunSearch improved, and can be evolved against delivery-rate benchmarks.
Utility scoring functions can be evolved as code against designer metrics (survival, need satisfaction, behavior variety), keeping the result readable unlike a neural policy.
Evolving solutions to each puzzle before launch estimates near-optimal cost, cycle or area scores, anchoring histogram axes and flagging degenerate puzzles.
Rivals or coaches could evolve programs in the game's own language against its evaluator, so player-written code competes with machine-evolved code under the same rules.

key_results.text: FunSearch found a cap set of size 512 in dimension 8 and online bin-packing heuristics that beat first fit and best fit on benchmark distributions.

AlphaEvolve found a 4x4 complex matrix multiplication with 48 scalar multiplications, matched about 75% and improved about 20% of over 50 open math problems, and produced a Borg scheduling heuristic that has recovered about 0.7% of Google's fleet compute in production for over a year.

Applied by Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner to 67 problems, AlphaEvolve mostly rediscovered the best known constructions, improved several, and sometimes generalized finite results into formulas.

Open-source successors lowered the barrier: ShinkaEvolve reported a new state-of-the-art circle packing with about 150 samples, and OpenEvolve runs the loop with any OpenAI-compatible or local model under Apache-2.0.

limitations: Requires a fast, automatic, trustworthy evaluator; anything judged by taste or fun has no such evaluator, and evolved code overfits whatever the evaluator measures.
Each run consumes thousands of LLM samples and program executions in earlier systems; ShinkaEvolve's roughly 150-sample result shows efficiency varies widely by problem.
Evolved heuristics are tuned to the benchmark instances and must be re-validated on new maps, content or patches.
No game studio use was found in this run's sources; all cited results are in mathematics, scheduling and systems code.
mechanism: A human supplies a program skeleton, the part to evolve (one priority function in FunSearch; arbitrary blocks across a file in AlphaEvolve), and an evaluator that runs a candidate and returns scores. A programs database holds evaluated programs; samplers build prompts from high-scoring and diverse parents and ask an LLM for a modified program; evaluators execute and score it; results flow back into the database. Diversity is kept with island populations (FunSearch) or MAP-Elites grids (OpenEvolve). Samplers and evaluators run asynchronously in parallel. The output is readable source code, so a discovered heuristic can be inspected, tested and shipped like hand-written code.
name: LLM-guided evolutionary program search
summary: An LLM proposes edits to code, an automated evaluator scores each candidate, and an evolutionary database keeps the best and most diverse programs, finding heuristics and constructions that beat human-designed ones.

affects.note: Agent pass rates plus a player-population model estimate how a difficulty ramp drives churn, so threat and difficulty curves can be tuned before release instead of from live telemetry.
Each scenario or level gets a predicted pass rate from human-like agents, letting designers order and adjust goals and constraints against a target difficulty curve.
Search agents measure how many actions each career path needs to reach each level, exposing careers that are much faster or slower than the rest, as in The Sims Mobile study.
Curiosity and RL agents explore traversal exhaustively, finding stuck spots, missing collision, and shortcuts that scripted navmesh bots do not reach.
Agents replaying the early game measure when resource and progression thresholds are reached, so unlock pacing is set from distributions instead of a few manual runs.
Agent playthroughs estimate win rates and dominant unit mixes in statistical combat before release.

key_results.text: King's CNN trained on player moves in Candy Crush Saga and Candy Crush Soda Saga predicted human moves and level difficulty, correlating better with average difficulty than MCTS at a fraction of the compute (IEEE CIG 2018).

EA used A* and evolution-strategy agents to balance The Sims Mobile careers during development and reported that deep RL needed heavy per-game tuning, so effort grew roughly linearly with the number of target games.

EA SEED's RL test agents found a wall missing its collision mesh that scripted navmesh agents missed and located all five stuck areas in a test map, and curiosity rewards raised coverage of a complex 3D map.

EA SEED added an experimental RL system to scripted-bot automated testing for AAA titles including Battlefield 2042 and Dead Space (2023) and reported that integration, not algorithms, consumed the most time.
RL agents combined with a player-population model of skill, persistence, and boredom predicted per-level pass and churn rates for Angry Birds Dream Blast.

SIMA 2 (2025) follows language instructions in commercial 3D games through screen input and virtual keyboard and mouse and transfers skills across games, but still struggles with long-horizon tasks, memory, and precise low-level control.

limitations: Agents are not players: skill and style differ, and imitation agents need large logs of real player moves, which a new game lacks before launch.
Integration dominates cost: EA SEED found engineering RL into production builds was the largest time sink, partly because development builds differ from the shipped game.
Deep RL transfers poorly between games without heavy hyperparameter tuning, so cost grows roughly linearly with the number of titles.
Open-ended simulation games have no single goal to optimize, so coverage or curiosity rewards stand in for design intent and can miss balance problems that only appear over long play.
mechanism: Agents play the game through an API or the rendered screen, in three families. Human-like agents are trained by supervised imitation of logged player moves, as with King's CNN on Candy Crush data, and their success rate on a new level predicts its difficulty for people. Goal-driven search or RL agents (A*, evolution strategies, deep RL) optimize task completion, and their action counts and success rates measure progression balance, as in EA's career-balancing study for The Sims Mobile. Curiosity agents are rewarded for novel states, maximizing map coverage to find stuck spots, missing collision, and unintended shortcuts. Agent results can feed a model of the player population: Roohi et al. combined RL agent pass rates with simulated skill, persistence, and boredom to predict per-level churn. In production, agents run against new builds inside the existing test pipeline and their coverage and failures are visualized for designers.
name: Agent-based automated playtesting and balancing
summary: Studios train imitation, reinforcement learning, and search agents to play builds, estimating level difficulty, pass and churn rates, progression pacing, map coverage, and exploits before players reach them.

affects.note: Candidate policies can be written as rule code in the game's own description language and screened by agent playouts for dominance and balance, so a policy list can be grown by search rather than authored one law at a time.
Laws players propose could be translated by a code model into enforceable rule code and run through the same compile and playout tests GAVEL uses, rejecting laws that fail to compile or break play.
Self-play over each generated variant measures first-player advantage, decisiveness, and the share of states with real choices, so turn order, phases, and move allowances can be adjusted by search.
End conditions are generated together with the rules and kept only if MCTS play reaches them without trivial draws or one-sided wins, replacing hand-tuned victory thresholds.
Generated content extends from text, items, and levels to complete executable rule sets that are compiled and filtered by playability and balance tests before anyone plays them.

key_results.text: Browne and Maire (IEEE TCIAIG 2010) evolved board game rule sets and ranked them with measures computed from self-play.
Ludii describes games with high-level ludemes and outperformed a propositional-network GDL reasoner on all games in the Tiltyard repository.

GAVEL (2024) fine-tuned CodeLlama-13b (about 40 hours on one RTX8000) on 574 Ludii games as a MAP-Elites mutation operator and generated playable games in rule-space regions not covered by existing Ludii games, scored by MCTS self-play metrics; samples are playable on the Ludii portal.
An LLM framework built on VGDL generated game rules and levels together, extending LLM generation from levels for fixed games to whole games.

limitations: Generated rule sets are small abstract board games; GAVEL trained on 574 games after removing those over 1,024 tokens, far below the size of a simulation game's rule base.
Self-play metrics such as balance, decisiveness, and agency describe agent play, not whether people enjoy the game, so human evaluation is still required.
Every candidate needs compilation plus random and MCTS playouts, so the search is offline and compute-bound.
Language models often emit rule code that fails to compile or is unplayable; GAVEL penalizes such candidates rather than preventing them.
Simulation games rarely have a formal rule language like Ludii or VGDL, so applying this needs the game's systems exposed as data or a scripting layer the generator can edit.
mechanism: Rules are written in a game description language. Ludii describes a game as a tree of ludemes (board, pieces, moves, end conditions) that compiles to a playable game; VGDL describes sprites, interactions, and termination for 2D video games. A generator proposes new rule trees: Browne and Maire's system evolved them by crossover and mutation, while GAVEL fine-tunes CodeLlama-13b with a fill-in-the-middle objective on 574 Ludii games and uses it as the mutation operator in MAP-Elites: a span of an existing game's rule code is masked and the model writes a replacement, and the archive is indexed by a 2D PCA projection of 510 Ludii concept features (1,600 cells). Candidates pass hierarchical tests (compiles, is playable, random playouts are not trivially one-sided and offer real choices) and are then scored by MCTS self-play on balance, decisiveness, completion, agency, coverage, and strategic depth. LLM frameworks built on VGDL generate rules and levels together from prompts. The output is a set of verified candidate rule sets for designers to play and select.
name: Automated generation of game rules and mechanics
summary: Systems that write complete game rule sets as code in a description language, using evolution or language models to propose rules and self-play agents to score balance, decisiveness, and strategic depth before a human sees them.

affects.note: Diplomacy becomes free-text negotiation with AI factions that propose specific joint moves, commit to them, and change plans when persuaded, instead of accept or decline treaty menus driven by opinion scores.
Typed messages are translated into predicted intents that feed a planner, so what the player says changes what the AI does on the map, and the AI's replies are constrained to match its own plan.

An AI that models what others expect it to do can also track whether the player's stated intentions matched their moves, turning standing into a learned estimate of trustworthiness rather than a scalar moved by scripted events.
Planner-grounded dialogue lets AI counterparties propose, counter, and keep terms in free text instead of accepting or rejecting fixed offers.
Peace terms could be negotiated in language against the war score, with the planner checking what the opponent will actually accept.

key_results.text: Cicero averaged more than double the human score over 40 games in an anonymous online Diplomacy league and ranked in the top 10% of participants who played more than one game (Science, November 2022).
Cicero pairs a controllable dialogue model with a planning engine that models other players' likely moves from the board and the conversation and predicts what others think Cicero will do.

The released code is MIT-licensed but model weights are CC-BY-NC 4.0, training scripts target a Slurm cluster (example configuration 256 GPUs), and the repository was archived read-only on 2025-04-17.
Richelieu (2024) built an LLM Diplomacy agent combining planning with memory and reflection, goal-directed negotiation, and self-play memory augmentation without human game data.

limitations: Built for one game: the dialogue model and the move policy were trained on human Diplomacy games and messages, so another game needs comparable data or a substitute.
Released weights are licensed for non-commercial use only (CC-BY-NC 4.0), and the repository is archived, so a studio cannot ship the released model.
Training assumed a GPU cluster (example 256 GPUs) and inference loads large models per agent, which is costly for a game with several AI factions per player.
Evaluation used an anonymous league; how players negotiate and whether they trust an opponent they know is an AI was not measured.
mechanism: Each phase, a planning module predicts every player's likely actions from the board state and the dialogue so far. It starts from a policy model trained on human games and refines it with piKL, a regret-minimization search regularized by a KL penalty toward the human-like policy, so predictions stay plausible while improving expected value. The resulting plan fixes intents: the actions Cicero intends to take and the actions it proposes to each recipient. A dialogue language model, trained on human game messages and conditioned on the board, the message history, and these intents, generates candidate messages, which are filtered for consistency with the plan and the game state. Incoming messages update the predicted intents of others, which changes the plan and therefore what Cicero says next. The planner also models what others expect Cicero to do. Because messages are generated from intents rather than freely, what Cicero says tracks what it plans to do.
name: Language models grounded in strategic planning for negotiation games
summary: Meta's Cicero couples a dialogue language model with a planning engine that infers other players' intentions from the board and conversation, so its free-text negotiation proposes and follows concrete joint plans, reaching human-level Diplomacy.

affects.note: Generated items, recipes, or characters can be written straight into typed game state (enum types, bounded stats, existing ids) instead of shown as text or parsed with retries, because invalid records cannot be emitted.
Free player text can be mapped onto the closed set of verbs and target ids legal in the current state, so conversation reliably triggers real game actions rather than only replies.

An LLM can be dropped into the action-selection slot by constraining it to choose among the same enumerated actions the utility scorer would rank, keeping the engine's action set and preconditions intact.
Card prompts, two to four options, and per-meter effect values can be generated in the game's card schema with effect sizes bounded by the grammar, leaving designers to curate rather than write.
Laws proposed in plain language can be compiled into the world's structured condition-and-effect rule language by grammar-constrained generation, so players need not learn the rule editor.

key_results.text: OpenAI's Structured Outputs (August 2024) reached 100% on a complex JSON-schema-following eval with gpt-4o-2024-08-06, versus under 40% for gpt-4-0613 without constraints.
XGrammar reports up to 100x faster grammar-constrained generation than prior engines and near-zero end-to-end overhead when integrated with an inference server.
Outlines showed that regex and CFG guidance can be implemented as finite-state-machine transitions with a precomputed vocabulary index and little per-token overhead.
Strict format restrictions such as JSON or XML significantly reduced LLM reasoning accuracy compared with free-form answers, with stricter formats causing larger drops.

Concordia's language-model interface includes a sample_choice call that scores a list of candidate responses and returns an index, raising an error after repeated invalid attempts, which is how its agents pick from closed option sets.
No source found documents constrained decoding in a specific shipped game; adoption in games is inferred from engine support (llama.cpp GBNF, hosted APIs) rather than observed.

limitations: Validity is not correctness: a well-formed action can still be the wrong action or reference stale state, so engines must re-check preconditions.
Format constraints can lower reasoning quality; a common workaround is free-form reasoning followed by a constrained final answer, which costs tokens.
Schema coverage varies: hosted APIs support a JSON Schema subset, and llama.cpp silently skips unsupported features such as nested $ref and uniqueItems and slows down with many optional items.
First use of a new schema adds compile latency (OpenAI reports under 10 seconds, up to a minute), so per-turn dynamic schemas need caching.
Output can still fail validation if generation hits a token limit.
mechanism: The output format (a JSON Schema, regular expression, or context-free grammar) is compiled into an automaton. At each decoding step the engine computes which vocabulary tokens keep the partial output a valid prefix and sets the logits of all others to minus infinity before sampling. Outlines precomputes an index from finite-state-machine states to allowed tokens; XGrammar handles full CFGs by prechecking context-independent tokens and checking context-dependent ones with a persistent stack, overlapping grammar work with GPU execution; hosted APIs convert schemas to CFGs and cache them; llama.cpp accepts GBNF grammars for local models. For games, the schema is built from current state: an enum of legal verbs, target ids that exist, and numeric fields with bounds, so every output maps to an action the engine can execute. A simpler variant scores a fixed list of candidate actions and returns the chosen index.
name: Grammar-constrained decoding for valid game actions
summary: Decoding that masks every token which cannot extend a valid string of a schema, regular expression, or grammar, so a model's output always parses as a legal game action or data record.

affects.note: In Flow-Lenia, rules travel with matter, so selection can act on creatures that emerge from the physics itself rather than on declared fitness stats.
Rule parameters mix where creatures meet in Flow-Lenia, giving inheritance and hybridization as a spatial process instead of an explicit genome crossover function.
ASAL turns a text prompt into a search over simulation rules that produce the described phenomenon, a route to generating new creature rule sets from player or designer descriptions at design time.

key_results.text: Lenia catalogued over 400 species in 18 families of geometric, segmented, resilient lifeforms, many found by interactive evolutionary search.
Flow-Lenia's mass conservation made localized creatures easier to find, and parameter localization let multiple species with different rules coexist and interact in one world.
ASAL found previously unseen Lenia and Boids lifeforms and open-ended cellular automata in the style of Game of Life, and quantified qualitative phenomena in ways that aligned with human judgment.

limitations: Lenia creatures exist in a narrow band of parameter space; most settings die out or explode, which is what made search tools necessary.
Creatures are fields without discrete identity, needs or stats, so connecting them to resource economies or player goals needs extra interpretation layers.
ASAL scores runs with a foundation model on rendered frames, which is offline-scale compute and inherits that model's notion of what looks interesting.
Open-ended evolution in these substrates is a stated aim, not an established result.
mechanism: Lenia stores a continuous field A(x) in [0,1]. Each step it convolves A with a smooth ring-shaped kernel K, passes the result through a bell-shaped growth function G, and updates A by a small time step dt times G(K*A), clipped to [0,1]; certain kernel and growth parameters yield moving, self-maintaining patterns ('species'). Flow-Lenia replaces additive growth with an affinity field that moves matter along its gradient, conserving total mass, and stores the rule parameters in the matter itself, so creatures carrying different rules can coexist, collide and mix. ASAL renders a simulation, embeds the frames with a vision-language foundation model, and scores parameter sets by similarity to a text prompt, by novelty of the embedding trajectory over time, or by diversity across a population; an evolutionary optimizer then searches the substrate's parameters (Boids, Particle Life, Game of Life, Lenia, NCA).
name: Continuous cellular automata and foundation-model search for artificial life
summary: Continuous cellular automata such as Lenia and mass-conserving Flow-Lenia produce lifelike self-organizing creatures, and ASAL uses vision-language foundation models to search their rule spaces for phenomena described in text or for open-ended novelty.

affects.note: AI drivers operate the same tire, suspension, and weight-transfer model as the player at champion level, so handling fidelity matters in races against the AI instead of being sidestepped by scripted racing lines.

Players practice against an opponent whose skill comes from the same controls and physics, at selectable levels (Beginner to Expert, then custom tire and fuel settings), raising the ceiling of a skill-centered mechanic.

For movement abilities such as grappling hooks, jetpacks, and double jumps, a learned policy replaces hand-placed navigation-mesh links, so NPCs can traverse spaces designers would otherwise annotate by hand.

key_results.text: GT Sophy, trained with model-free deep RL across mixed racing scenarios and a reward designed around sportsmanship rules, beat four of the world's best Gran Turismo drivers head to head (Nature, February 2022).

GT Sophy entered Gran Turismo 7 as the time-limited Race Together event in update 1.29 (February 2023), with four races against GT Sophy cars of different performance at Beginner, Intermediate, and Expert levels and a 1vs1 mode.
GT Sophy 2.0 became a permanent Quick Race rival in GT7's Spec II update (November 2023) on nine tracks and 340 cars, 95% of the car models, up from four cars and four tracks, on PS5 only.
GT Sophy 2.1 (update 1.57, March 2025) moved into Custom Race with 19 car and track options, lap count, parts and tuning changes, and adjustable tire and fuel consumption.

Ubisoft La Forge's deep RL navigation handled grappling hooks, jetpacks, teleporters, and double jumps on maps about ten times larger than typical RL research maps, one modeled on a Ubisoft AAA game, with at least 90% success.
Unity's open-source ML-Agents Toolkit lets developers train agents inside Unity scenes.

limitations: Coverage arrives per content item: GT Sophy grew from four cars and four tracks to nine tracks and 340 cars across updates, because each track and car needs training and validation.

A policy trained to win needs reward shaping and later refinement for sportsmanship and enjoyment; Sony AI describes refining GT Sophy's behavior for etiquette and players of all skill levels after the research version.
Availability was narrow at first: GT Sophy 2.0 ran only in Quick Race on PS5, not in other events on the same tracks.
Learned policies are hard to direct for scripted moments, and physics or content patches can require retraining and re-validation.
Deep RL transfers poorly between games without heavy tuning, as EA reported, so each title builds its own training setup.
mechanism: The game exposes observations (car state, track geometry, nearby opponents; or local terrain and goal direction for navigation) and actions (steering, throttle, brake; or movement and ability inputs) to a learning agent. Many instances run in parallel, and model-free deep RL learns a policy network that maps observations to actions to maximize a shaped reward. For GT Sophy the reward values course progress and was designed to encode racing's under-specified sportsmanship rules, and training mixed racing scenarios so one policy handles both speed and tactics. For NPCs with jetpacks, grappling hooks, or double jumps, where navigation meshes break down, the reward is reaching a goal. The trained network is small enough to run every frame. Difficulty is set by giving the agent cars of different performance or alternate checkpoints, and later GT Sophy versions expose settings such as tire and fuel consumption. Toolkits such as Unity ML-Agents connect engine scenes to training code.
name: Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation
summary: Neural control policies trained with deep reinforcement learning inside the game's own simulation drive opponents and NPCs, as with Sony AI's Gran Turismo Sophy, a selectable rival in Gran Turismo 7 since 2023.

affects.note: The gradient of a design's rating with respect to each part parameter tells the player which strut, joint or track segment most changes the score, enabling hints like 'move this support left'.
Material stiffness and damping of node-beam or finite-element bodies can be fitted to reference motion or a target feel by gradient descent, as DiffTaichi does for elastic objects.
Tire, suspension and drivetrain constants can be fitted to recorded telemetry by differentiating lap or trajectory error, replacing manual parameter sweeps.
GradABM shows transmission parameters of a million-agent outbreak model calibrated to real case data by gradients, a route to epidemic games whose curves match real diseases or designer targets.
Differentiable fluid kernels (Warp, DiffTaichi) allow inverse design, solving for emitter or vent settings that produce a target flow, usable for level authoring or tuning puzzles.
A controller for a player-built soft or articulated body can be optimized in tens of gradient iterations, so assembled machines can learn to walk or swim during play.

key_results.text: DiffTaichi implemented 10 differentiable simulators; its elastic-object simulator was 4.2x shorter than hand-written CUDA at similar speed and 188x faster than a TensorFlow version, and neural controllers optimized in tens of iterations.
Brax exposed gradients through a JAX rigid-body engine running at millions of steps per second on one accelerator.
NVIDIA Warp lets developers write differentiable GPU kernels in Python; NVIDIA reports Autodesk fluid simulations 8x faster and 5x larger than with traditional frameworks.
GradABM made a million-agent epidemic agent-based model differentiable, ran it in a few seconds on commodity hardware, and calibrated it to COVID-19 and influenza data by gradient descent.
As of 2026, gradient support is uneven across GPU engines: MuJoCo Warp lists differentiability via Warp as not yet available.

limitations: Collisions, contact switching, and integer or threshold game rules give zero, undefined, or misleading gradients and need smoothing or relaxations that change the dynamics being tuned.
Reverse-mode differentiation must store or recompute intermediate states, so memory grows with timesteps times state size; long horizons also produce exploding or vanishing gradients.
Support is incomplete in production-grade GPU engines; MuJoCo Warp lists differentiability via Warp as not yet available.
Gradient descent finds local optima of a stated loss; matching a target curve is not the same as making a system fun or balanced.
mechanism: The simulator step is written in a language with automatic differentiation: source-transformed kernels (DiffTaichi, NVIDIA Warp) or traced array programs (JAX in Brax). A loss is defined on the final or accumulated state, for example distance of a soft robot from a goal or error between simulated and observed infection counts. Reverse-mode differentiation propagates the gradient back through every timestep to the parameters, which are updated by gradient descent. Contacts and discrete events are smoothed or given surrogate gradients. For agent-based models, agent state is held in tensors and stochastic discrete events are replaced by differentiable relaxations so the whole population update has gradients (GradABM). The payoff is that tuning takes tens of gradient iterations instead of thousands of blind rollouts.
name: Differentiable simulation
summary: Simulators written so automatic differentiation returns gradients of an outcome with respect to initial state, controls, or rule parameters, replacing black-box search with gradient descent for tuning and inverse design.

affects.note: Avatar movement, camera response, and weapon use are predicted frame by frame from keyboard and mouse input instead of computed by engine code; responsiveness depends on denoising steps and frame rate (20 fps GameNGen and Oasis, about 10 fps DIAMOND CS:GO).
Collision, gravity, and jumping are learned statistically from pixels rather than integrated; rules the data rarely violates can still be broken, as with DIAMOND's repeated mid-air jumps in CS:GO.

Terrain is invented on demand from the learned distribution of the training game with no seed or noise function (Oasis), but it is not persistent: regions that leave the short context window are regenerated differently on return.

Every frame, enemy, and pickup is generated content conditioned on play, so a game can in principle contain situations its source game never had; in practice output stays inside the training game's distribution.

In Oasis and MineWorld, breaking and placing Minecraft blocks is predicted as pixels with no stored voxel grid, so edits are not durable; Oasis placing a dirt block can bring up an entirely different environment.

key_results.text: GameNGen simulates DOOM at 20 frames per second on a single TPU, with next-frame PSNR of 29.43; human raters picked the real game over the simulation only 58 percent (1.6 s clips) and 60 percent (3.2 s clips) of the time.

GameNGen conditions on 64 past frames (about 3 seconds) and was trained on about 70M frames recorded from a PPO agent trained for 50M environment steps; the authors state the model cannot be used to create new games.

DIAMOND reached a mean human-normalized score of 1.46 on Atari 100k for agents trained entirely inside a diffusion world model, and a CS:GO world model trained on 87 hours of human play runs at about 10 fps on an RTX 3090 but lets the player jump repeatedly in mid-air, which the real game forbids.

Oasis (Decart and Etched, October 2024) generated a Minecraft-like open world at 20 fps in a public browser demo with 500M-parameter open weights; reviewers found the layout rearranged after turning around, and Decart did not say it had Microsoft's permission to train on Minecraft footage.
MineWorld (Microsoft Research, 2025) released an open visual-action autoregressive transformer for Minecraft that generates 4 to 7 frames per second depending on model scale.

limitations: Memory is a few seconds: GameNGen's 64-frame context covers about 3 seconds, and Oasis shows about 3 seconds of memory in one example, so off-screen state such as map layout or enemy positions is lost.
Requires an existing game to record: GameNGen needed about 70M agent frames from DOOM, DIAMOND 87 hours of CS:GO play; the approach clones a game rather than authoring a new one.

Each player needs a dedicated accelerator (one TPU-v5 for GameNGen, H100s for Oasis); Maginative reports cost remains a significant barrier to deploying such models at scale, and no per-player-hour figure is published.
State such as health, ammo, inventory, and score is only as reliable as the pixels that show it; Oasis inventory control is imprecise and distant geometry is fuzzy.
Training on footage of commercial games raises unresolved licensing questions.
mechanism: A game is recorded as pairs of frames and player actions (from an RL agent in GameNGen, human play in DIAMOND's CS:GO model, or gameplay video in Oasis). A generator is trained to predict frame t+1 from the last N frames and the action at t: a latent diffusion model in GameNGen, DIAMOND, and Oasis, or a transformer over interleaved image and action tokens in MineWorld. Context frames are noised during training (noise augmentation, Diffusion Forcing, dynamic noising) so the model can recover from its own errors during long rollouts, and sampling is cut to a few denoising steps for real-time play. There is no explicit game state: position, health, enemies, and map layout exist only as pixels or latents inside the context window, so anything that leaves the window is forgotten unless it is visible on screen.
name: Diffusion and autoregressive neural game engines
summary: Action-conditioned generative models trained on recordings of one existing game predict each next frame from recent frames and player input, so the model itself plays the role of the game engine.

affects.note: PhysGaussian deforms captured objects with MPM directly on the rendered Gaussians, so a scanned real object can bend, dent, or flow without building a node-beam or finite-element mesh first.

Photoreal props and scenery can be captured from photos in under an hour of training instead of modeled and textured by hand, enlarging decor catalogs that beauty scores consume; lighting is baked into the capture.

key_results.text: Kerbl et al. (2023) reached real-time (30 fps or more) novel-view synthesis at 1080p with state-of-the-art visual quality and competitive training times.

A full 3DGS scene trains in about 35 to 45 minutes versus about 48 hours for Mip-NeRF 360, but uses more memory than NeRF methods, with peak training memory over 20 GB, and shows popping and elongated-splat artifacts.

PhysGaussian simulates elastic, metal, non-Newtonian, and granular behavior directly on Gaussian kernels with an MPM solver, avoiding meshing so the simulated and rendered representation are the same.

Khronos released a KHR_gaussian_splatting glTF 2.0 extension as a release candidate on 2026-02-03 with contributors including Autodesk, Cesium, Esri, Niantic Spatial, and NVIDIA, expecting ratification in Q2 2026.
Generated-world products export splats as their highest-fidelity format and render them in the browser (World Labs Marble with the Spark renderer).

limitations: Colors store captured radiance, so lighting is baked in; dynamic time of day, player-placed lights, and relighting are not supported by the base method.
Memory heavy: millions of Gaussians per scene and training peaks above 20 GB.
No collision geometry or semantics: gameplay needs separate meshes or proxies for physics and pathfinding.
Editing and stylizing splats is harder than editing meshes; tooling and a ratified interchange standard were still arriving in 2026.
mechanism: Starting from sparse structure-from-motion points, each Gaussian stores position, anisotropic covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color as spherical harmonics. A differentiable tile-based rasterizer projects, depth-sorts, and alpha-blends the Gaussians; gradients from photo reconstruction error update parameters while adaptive density control splits, clones, and prunes Gaussians. Rendering needs no neural network at runtime, so it runs at real-time rates. Extensions attach physics directly to the Gaussians (PhysGaussian runs a Material Point Method on the kernels), stream level-of-detail on the web, and standardize the format in glTF.
name: 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Scenes are represented as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians optimized from photos and rasterized in real time, giving photoreal captured or generated environments at 1080p and 30+ fps.

affects.note: A companion can take open-ended spoken or typed orders, sketches, or emoji and carry them out with ordinary game controls, so the command vocabulary is no longer limited to the verbs a designer bound to buttons.
The player can hand an avatar or task to an agent that pursues a stated goal in any game it can see, without game-specific AI code, and that explains what it intends to do.
SIMA 2 converses about its surroundings, answers questions about the scene, and explains its actions, grounding dialogue in what it sees on screen.
Self-improving agents that advance through a game's tech tree can serve as automated playtesters of progression in builds they were not trained on.
Agents that follow language instructions and watch play could learn routines from a single narrated demonstration instead of recorded literal steps.

key_results.text: SIMA 1 learned about 600 basic skills across Valheim, Teardown, No Man's Sky, Wobbly Life, Satisfactory, Goat Simulator 3, Hydroneer, Space Engineers, and Eco; the multi-game agent outperformed per-game specialists, and an agent trained without one game performed nearly as well on it as a specialist.
SIMA 1 tasks completed in about 10 seconds and the agent could not do multi-step strategic planning.

SIMA 2 roughly doubled SIMA 1's average task success on training games, approaching human players, and beat SIMA 1 by over 10% on held-out ASKA and MineDojo, completing tasks in 26 of 50 MineDojo categories.

Through self-generated tasks and rewards in ASKA, SIMA 2 went from succeeding on under a quarter of a fixed task set to exceeding human reference scores and progressed further through ASKA's tech tree than earlier versions.
SIMA 2 was released only as a limited research preview to a small group of academics and game developers.

limitations: Weak combat and precise low-level control; failures in held-out games are often due to poor exploration.
Short memory bounded by the context window, and trouble with long multi-step tasks that need goal verification.
Built on Gemini Flash-Lite for latency; fine-tuning cost general reasoning (about 25.5% drop on AIME after SFT).
Runs as a cloud model reading the screen, so per-session inference cost and round-trip latency apply; no public cost figures.
Not available to players; the reward model was calibrated on a small set of trajectories.
mechanism: The agent sees only rendered frames and a language instruction and emits keyboard and mouse actions in real time, with no access to game source, state APIs, or per-game reward code. SIMA (2024) was trained on human gameplay with language annotations across nine commercial games and four research environments covering about 600 short skills (navigate, interact with objects, use menus). SIMA 2 (2025) puts a fine-tuned Gemini Flash-Lite model at the core, so the agent reasons about goals, states its plan, converses, and follows sketches or emoji. It then improves without human data: a Gemini task setter proposes tasks likely achievable from the current state, the agent attempts them, a Gemini reward model scores each trajectory from 0 to 100 (50 or more counts as success), and the agent trains on the scored experience.
name: Generalist instructable game agents (SIMA)
summary: Agents that read screen pixels and natural-language instructions and output keyboard and mouse actions across many commercial 3D games, with later versions reasoning, conversing, and improving through self-generated tasks.

affects.note: Maps come from a prompt, photo, or video rather than a seed and noise pipeline, and unlike frame-based world models the result is baked geometry that persists, can be saved, and can be expanded region by region.
Bespoke scenario maps can be produced from a reference image or description and exported with collider meshes, reducing hand modeling per scenario; objectives and rules still need authoring.

Chisel turns a coarse blockout into a detailed styled scene, the same rough-input to detailed-output contract as Townscaper-style build assist but with a learned generator; today it is an editor mode, not a runtime player tool.
Exported collider meshes give generated scenes collision geometry automatically; Marble describes them as coarse, so precise physics still needs cleanup.

key_results.text: Marble became generally available on 2025-11-12, taking text, images, video, or coarse 3D layouts and exporting Gaussian splats, triangle meshes including collider meshes for coarse physics, and rendered video; Chisel separates blocked-out structure from prompted style.

HunyuanWorld 1.0 (Tencent, July 2025) generates explorable worlds from text or images via panoramic proxies converted to a semantically layered 3D mesh exportable to standard graphics pipelines, listing game development as an application.
RTFM (October 2025) renders generated or real scenes from a single image at interactive frame rates on one H100, using posed frames as spatial memory; it models static scenes only.
World Labs launched a public World API in January 2026, released Atlas to early-access partners in September 2026, and announced it is joining AMD on 2026-09-28.

limitations: Scenes are static: no dynamic objects, agents, or rules are generated, and RTFM lists dynamics and interaction as future work.
Single-image or text prompts force the model to invent unseen regions; Marble notes artifacts and less crisp far regions that expansion may fix.
Splat output bakes lighting into colors, so day-night cycles and relighting need conversion to meshes or other methods.
Collider meshes are coarse and need manual work for gameplay-critical collision.
Corporate change (World Labs joining AMD in 2026) leaves the hosted product's future terms uncertain.
mechanism: An image or video diffusion model generates views of a scene (a 360-degree panorama in HunyuanWorld, multi-view images in Marble) from the prompt; the views are lifted to an explicit 3D representation (3D Gaussian splats, or a semantically layered mesh) that can be walked through and re-rendered without regeneration. Marble also emits triangle meshes and coarse collider meshes for physics, can expand or merge worlds, and in Chisel mode takes a blockout of boxes and planes as structure and a text prompt as style. A parallel line renders frames directly instead of building geometry: RTFM keeps generated frames with camera poses as spatial memory and retrieves nearby frames as context. Atlas (2026) is a multimodal model that outputs video, point clouds, and splats.
name: Prompt-to-persistent 3D world generation
summary: Models such as World Labs Marble and HunyuanWorld turn text, images, video, or coarse 3D blockouts into persistent explorable scenes exported as Gaussian splats and meshes with collision proxies.

affects.note: Memories become free-text records with LLM-rated importance, retrieved by recency, importance, and relevance, plus reflections that summarize many records into beliefs, instead of a fixed catalog of timed mood modifiers.

Each agent writes its own day plan from its description and memories, decomposed into hour and 5-15 minute steps and revised on events, in place of authored routine tables; the player still sees rhythms of work, meals, and leisure.

The next action is chosen by prompting with the current plan step, perceived surroundings, and retrieved memories rather than by scoring options against need curves, so choices can reference past events and other agents.

Information moves through generated conversations whose content comes from memory retrieval, so what spreads, to whom, and how it is reworded emerge from dialogue; in Smallville party awareness rose from 4% to 52% of agents with 1.3% hallucinated answers.

Relationships are held as remembered interactions and reflections about another agent rather than a numeric affinity, so a relationship's state is a set of retrievable facts; Smallville's acquaintance network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74 in two days.
Agents open-endedly converse, invite, and coordinate (for example planning and attending a party) without a predefined catalog of social moves and preconditions.

Because an agent's state is natural-language memories, plans, and reflections, the player or designer can read them directly or interview the agent about why it acted, which is how the original paper evaluated believability.
Memory streams summarized at low frequency give off-screen characters histories that persist when the player returns.
Wants generated from an agent's own memories and reflections rather than rolled from a fixed table tied to an aspiration.

key_results.text: In Smallville, 25 agents on gpt-3.5-turbo were rated for believability by 100 human raters (TrueSkill): full architecture 29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, human crowdworkers role-playing 22.95, no memory, planning, or reflection 21.21.

Over two game days, knowledge of a seeded party spread from 1 to 13 of 25 agents and of a mayoral candidacy from 1 to 8, network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74, five of twelve invited agents attended the party, and 1.3% of 453 awareness answers were hallucinated.
The simulation cost thousands of dollars in token credits and took multiple days of wall-clock time for 25 agents.

Affordable Generative Agents used 31.1% of the baseline's tokens for a 3-agent town over two game days and 42.7% for the 25-agent town, by replaying cached plan-action policies (embedding match at cosine 0.97) and compressing about 2,000 prompt tokens of social context to about 100.

NVIDIA describes inZOI's Smart Zois as agents that plan, act, and reflect on their decisions using small language models, and inZOI's Steam disclosure says character actions and thoughts can be influenced through an on-device SLM.

limitations: Cost and wall-clock time: 25 agents over two game days cost thousands of dollars and took days to run on gpt-3.5-turbo (2023 prices).
Retrieval failures and embellishment: agents sometimes miss relevant memories or add fabricated details to recalled events.
Instruction-tuned models make agents overly formal and cooperative, and agents misread location norms such as single-occupancy bathrooms or closing hours.

Each agent step is several sequential LLM calls (importance rating, retrieval-conditioned action, dialogue, reflection), so per-agent latency is seconds, which limits real-time populations unless calls are cached or batched.
Behavior is not reproducible from a seed with hosted models; replays and saves must store generated outputs.
mechanism: Each agent appends observations as natural-language records to a memory stream. To act or speak, it retrieves records by a score that sums min-max normalized recency (exponential decay, factor 0.995 per game hour), importance (an LLM rating from 1 to 10 made when the record is stored), and relevance (embedding cosine similarity to the current situation), all with weight 1. When the summed importance of recent records exceeds 150, roughly two or three times a game day, the agent asks the LLM for high-level questions and inferences and stores the answers as reflections that can be retrieved like observations. Planning is top-down: a daily sketch is decomposed into hour chunks and then 5-15 minute actions, and the plan is revised when a perceived event warrants a reaction. Dialogue is generated from retrieved memories about the other agent. Cost-reduction variants replay stored plan-action sequences when a new plan matches an old one by embedding similarity and compress social context into short summaries, cutting LLM calls.
name: Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning)
summary: LLM-driven characters that store observations in a natural-language memory stream, retrieve them by recency, importance, and relevance, synthesize reflections, and plan their day top-down.

affects.note: Genie 3's promptable world events change weather by text during a session with no weather simulation or authored weather assets; the change is visual only and has no stored state for crops, agents, or travel to read.

A director could inject an event (a new character, object, or condition) as a text prompt that Genie 3 renders into the running world, removing per-event art and animation; event selection and pacing still need a separate system with real state.

Worlds come from a text or image prompt instead of a seed and noise pipeline, in any visual style; persistence is minutes long (about one minute of visual memory in Genie 3, 60-second sessions in Project Genie).
First- or third-person character movement is rendered by the model from WASD, camera, and jump input; the action space is small and collisions are not guaranteed (characters passing through walls).

Object responses such as doors opening, balloons bursting, water, and smoke are produced by learned video dynamics (Genie 2) rather than a physics engine, with no conservation or collision guarantees.
Whole explorable scenes, characters, and events are generated at runtime from player text, sketches, or photos, which extends generative content from text and items to playable space.

Promptable world events work as a free-form god power: typed text adds characters, objects, or weather to the running world; Genie 3 attaches no cost or rule to them and their effects exist only in rendered frames.

key_results.text: Genie has 11B parameters trained on 30k hours of 2D platformer clips with 8 latent actions; it generates about 1 frame per second and has 16 frames of memory, which the paper lists as limitations.
Genie 2 turns one image into a playable 3D world with water, smoke, gravity, lighting, door opening, and NPCs; worlds stay coherent for up to a minute, but most examples last 10 to 20 seconds.

Genie 3 renders 720p at 24 fps in real time, stays consistent for a few minutes with visual memory reaching back about one minute, and supports text prompts that change weather or add objects and characters mid-session; DeepMind lists limited action space and multi-agent interaction as open problems.

Project Genie opened Genie 3 to US Google AI Ultra subscribers on 2026-01-29 with a 60-second limit per world set by compute cost; a reviewer saw characters walk through walls and sometimes unresponsive controls, and copyrighted settings were refused.
Shares of video game companies, including Unity, fell after the Project Genie launch.
Waymo built a world model on Genie 3 (February 2026) to simulate driving edge cases, controllable by driving action, scene layout, and language.

limitations: Session length: Genie 2 coherence is usually 10 to 20 seconds; Genie 3 manages a few minutes; Project Genie caps exploration at 60 seconds because of compute.
No inspectable state: there are no variables for inventory, health, or object identity, so mechanics that need stocks or rules must live in a separate system.
Limited action space and no reliable multi-agent interaction (DeepMind's stated Genie 3 limitations).
Access is a hosted research prototype for paying subscribers; no public API, price per hour, or on-device version is published.
Guardrails refuse copyrighted settings and nudity, which constrains user-generated worlds.
mechanism: Genie (2024) learned from 30k hours of unlabeled 2D platformer video: a video tokenizer, a latent action model that infers 8 discrete actions between frames without labels, and a 10.1B-parameter dynamics model that predicts the next frame tokens given an action. Genie 2 (December 2024) is an autoregressive latent diffusion model with a transformer dynamics model that turns a single image into a 3D world controlled by keyboard and mouse. Genie 3 (August 2025) generates frames auto-regressively in real time from a text prompt, keeps visual memory of earlier frames for about a minute so revisited places look the same, and accepts text 'promptable world events' during play that add objects, characters, or weather changes. No explicit 3D scene or game state is stored; consistency comes from the frame history.
name: Genie foundation world models
summary: Google DeepMind's Genie models generate playable worlds from a text or image prompt and render them in real time from player input, with Genie 3 reaching 720p at 24 fps and about a minute of visual memory.

affects.note: Learned fluid surrogates (GNS particles, FNO fields) reproduce solver-quality flow at large speedups, raising resolution or extent of water and gas within a frame budget.
MeshGraphNets predicts cloth and structural deformation 10-100x faster than its training solver, allowing finite-element-like deformation where games now use coarse node-beam models.
GNS simulates several materials (fluids, rigid solids, deformables) interacting in one learned model, so mixed-material reactions need no hand-written pairwise rules.
MeshGraphNets learned aerodynamic flow around airfoils, pointing to flight models driven by surrogate CFD fields instead of fixed lift and drag coefficient tables.
Learned structural-mechanics surrogates output stress and deformation fields, which could replace binary support checks with graded bending, sagging and stress-driven failure.
Neural operators solve parametric flow PDEs in one forward pass at any grid resolution, a candidate replacement for per-cell iterative water-flow updates over large terrains.

key_results.text: GNS learned fluids, rigid solids and deformable materials as interacting particles; models trained on single steps with thousands of particles generalized to thousands of rollout steps and at least 10x more particles.
MeshGraphNets predicted cloth, structural mechanics and aerodynamics on adaptive meshes and ran 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than the simulator it was trained on.
The Fourier Neural Operator modeled Navier-Stokes turbulence with zero-shot super-resolution and was up to three orders of magnitude faster than traditional PDE solvers.

limitations: Errors accumulate over long rollouts; GNS needed training-noise injection to stay stable, and nothing guarantees conservation of mass or energy.
Each material or domain needs a training set generated by a numerical solver, and behavior outside the training distribution (new materials, extreme speeds, novel geometry) is unreliable.
Reported speedups are against the high-accuracy solver used for training, not against the cheap approximations games already ship, so the net gain for a game can be much smaller.
Inference runs on the GPU and competes with rendering for the frame budget.
Results are cited from 2020-2021 primary papers; this run found no shipped game using GNS or neural operators at runtime.
mechanism: Graph network simulators treat particles (GNS) or mesh vertices (MeshGraphNets) as nodes, with edges to neighbors within a radius or along mesh connectivity. An encoder embeds positions, velocities and material type; several rounds of learned message passing compute pairwise interactions; a decoder outputs per-node accelerations that a simple integrator applies. Models are trained on one-step targets from a numerical solver, with noise added to inputs so long rollouts stay stable. MeshGraphNets also learns where to refine the mesh. Neural operators such as the Fourier Neural Operator learn a map from one function to another (for example initial vorticity to vorticity at a later time) by applying learned kernels in Fourier space, so one model covers a family of PDE instances and can be evaluated at grid resolutions not seen in training.
name: Graph network simulators and neural operators
summary: Learned simulators that predict the next state of particles, meshes, or continuous fields with message-passing networks or Fourier-space operators, trained on numerical solver output and run 10-1000x faster than that solver.

affects.note: Customer purchase decisions could be sampled from a model trained on human choice data, giving realistic heterogeneity and biases, instead of utility = value x preference - price with hand-set weights.
Visitor populations could be drawn from person-grounded profiles whose preferences and tolerances are measured against real people rather than sampled from designer distributions.
Simulated electorates could be built from survey-grounded agents that reproduce subgroup opinion distributions, so vote shares respond to issues the way measured populations do.
A group's preferences over policies could be derived from simulated members (silicon samples) rather than a single authored ideology vector.
A character's disposition can be a rich text profile whose predicted Big Five scores and economic-game behavior match a real respondent, rather than a few discrete trait tags.
Before ship, designers could estimate option pick rates for each card by querying a choice model on the card text; untested on game content.
Counterparties whose acceptance follows models of human bargaining (fairness, anchoring) rather than a single reservation price.
Segment-level response to advertising predicted from models of human choice instead of a flat awareness multiplier.
Mode-choice weights for time, cost, and comfort can be fitted to predicted human choices instead of hand-set.

key_results.text: Agents built from two-hour interviews with 1,052 U.S. adults replicated General Social Survey answers 85% as accurately as participants replicated their own answers two weeks later, and performed comparably on Big Five traits, five economic games, and five experiments, with smaller accuracy gaps across racial and ideological groups than demographics-only agents.
The later arXiv version reports normalized GSS accuracy of 83% for interview-only, 82% survey-only, 86% combined, and 74% demographics-only agents.

Centaur predicted held-out participants better than 14 cognitive and statistical models and generalized to new cover stories, structural task changes, and new domains; the authors propose it for in silico prototyping of experiments.

With task instructions removed or replaced by misleading ones, Centaur still generally beat domain-specific cognitive models, which its critics read as reliance on statistical cues rather than understanding the task.

Earlier work showed GPT-3 conditioned on survey backstories reproduces subgroup response distributions (algorithmic fidelity), while GPT-4-era models replicated classic experiments but showed a hyper-accuracy distortion on wisdom-of-crowds questions.

limitations: Psych-101 is skewed toward WEIRD participants and toward learning and decision-making tasks; individual differences such as age were not in the prompts.
Critics show Centaur performs well even without valid instructions, so its predictions on new game situations may track surface statistics.
Interview-grounded agents need hours of data per person, which raises consent and privacy questions for player data.
Centaur's 70B base needed about five days on one A100 to fine-tune; the 8B Minitaur variant generalized less robustly.
No study yet validates these models on choices inside games, where options are visual, timed, and repeated.
mechanism: Two approaches. Grounded agents put a person's two-hour interview transcript (or survey answers) in the prompt of a generative agent and ask it to answer new questions as that person; accuracy is normalized by how consistently the real person answers the same items two weeks later. Fine-tuned choice models transcribe experiments into natural language and train a model to predict each trial's choice: Centaur adds rank-8 QLoRA adapters (about 0.15% of parameters) to a frozen 4-bit Llama 3.1 70B and trains one epoch on Psych-101 (160 experiments, 60,092 participants, 10,681,650 choices), scoring held-out participants by negative log-likelihood against cognitive models. Earlier silicon-sample work conditions a model on demographic backstories to reproduce subgroup response distributions. In games the same pipeline would predict how players or simulated citizens choose among options described in text.
name: LLM models of individual human choice
summary: Language models conditioned on interviews or fine-tuned on millions of experimental choices that predict how specific people or populations answer surveys, play economic games, and choose in decision tasks.

affects.note: AI players reason over unseen state as a belief distribution and play strategies that are hard to exploit, instead of cheating with full map knowledge or ignoring hidden units, so concealment and feints work against the AI as they would against a person.

Equilibrium strategies put a value on information, so AI opponents scout, hide their own attributes, and avoid revealing them through their actions, giving the player's scouting system a real counterpart.
AI bidders play mixed strategies over private valuations instead of bidding a fixed fraction of value, which removes simple exploits such as always outbidding the AI by one unit.

Deception becomes a stable part of AI play, as DeepNash bluffed with hidden unit identities in Stratego, so operational wargames could field opponents that feint and conceal force composition at calibrated rates.
Competitors with private costs or plans can bluff in price wars and market entry, and designers can measure how exploitable a fixed AI pricing script is by computing a best response against it.
Bargaining with hidden reservation values is an imperfect-information game; equilibrium strategies bluff and concede in ways scripted thresholds cannot.

key_results.text: Libratus beat top professionals at heads-up no-limit Texas hold'em (Science, January 2018).
DeepStack beat professional players with statistical significance over 44,000 hands of heads-up no-limit hold'em using recursive re-solving with a learned value function.

Pluribus beat elite professionals at six-player no-limit hold'em, winning about 5 big blinds per 100 hands over 10,000 hands; its blueprint took 8 days of Monte Carlo CFR on a 64-core server (under $150 of cloud compute) and it played on two CPUs at about 20 seconds per hand.
ReBeL combined self-play RL with search, provably converging to a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games, and reached superhuman heads-up no-limit hold'em with less domain knowledge.
DeepNash reached a top-3 all-time ranking among expert humans on the Gravon Stratego platform using model-free Regularised Nash Dynamics and no search (Science, December 2022).

Student of Games (Science Advances, November 2023) used one sound algorithm across chess, Go, heads-up no-limit poker, and Scotland Yard, beating the strongest openly available poker agent and the prior best Scotland Yard agent.

limitations: Convergence guarantees hold for two-player zero-sum games; Pluribus's six-player play works empirically without them, and cooperative or general-sum simulation games fall outside the theory.
Large games need designed abstractions of actions and states; a simulation with continuous economies and many units has no obvious abstraction to solve.
Runtime search costs seconds per decision (Pluribus averaged about 20 seconds per hand on two CPUs), far above per-frame budgets for many agents.
Equilibrium play avoids being exploited rather than exploiting weak players, which can feel passive, and randomized bluffs read as arbitrary unless the game explains them.
mechanism: A decision point is an information set: all histories the player cannot tell apart. CFR traverses the game tree repeatedly; at each information set it computes each action's counterfactual regret (how much better it would have done, weighted by the probability that others reach that set) and sets the next strategy by regret matching, proportional to positive cumulative regret. The average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games, and Monte Carlo CFR samples the tree to scale. Large games are abstracted (bucketed hands and bet sizes) into an offline blueprint that is refined during play by subgame search: Libratus used nested subgame solving, DeepStack re-solved to a depth limit with a learned value function, and Pluribus searched a few moves ahead while letting each opponent pick among four continuation strategies at the leaves. ReBeL and Student of Games learn values over public belief states and search with them, reducing to AlphaZero-style search in perfect-information games. DeepNash instead learns a policy model-free with Regularised Nash Dynamics and no search. Outputs are mixed strategies, so the agent bluffs at calibrated rates.
name: Regret minimization and search for imperfect-information games
summary: Self-play algorithms that minimize counterfactual regret over information sets, refined by real-time subgame search, compute hard-to-exploit strategies that bluff and hide information and beat top humans at poker, Stratego, and Scotland Yard.

affects.note: Hand-written noise and placement rules give way to a generator trained on example maps or prompted with text, so a seed becomes a prompt plus a sample, and validity must be checked by a solver instead of guaranteed by construction.
Scenario maps can be produced from a written description of the situation, Word2World-style story to world, with an agent playthrough confirming the stated goal is reachable.

Difficulty-conditioned generators let the next map or wave be built at a target difficulty instead of multiplying enemy counts, though EA SEED's match-3 model hit the requested difficulty only a third of the time.
Text-to-level models small enough to run on the client (MarioGPT has 96M parameters) let players request maps in words at runtime, extending generated content from text and items to playable space.

key_results.text: PCGRL (2020) framed level design as a Markov decision process with three editing representations tested on three games, giving a fast generator that needs few or no example levels.

MarioGPT (2023) fine-tuned a 96M-parameter DistilGPT2 model on 37 Super Mario Bros levels; 88.4% of 250 generated levels were completed by an A* agent versus about 31% for an LSTM baseline, and output followed text prompts.
LLM Sokoban level generation improved sharply with training-set size, and scarce level data was the main obstacle (FDG 2023).
Word2World (2024) used off-the-shelf LLMs without fine-tuning to write a story and place tiles into a coherent, playable 2D world.

EA SEED's difficulty-conditioned match-3 generator produced 51.39% valid levels versus 46.15% in its training data, but matched the requested difficulty only 33.33% of the time (mean gap 10.19 moves).
ARLPCG trained a generator adversarially against a solver agent in a 3D platformer and a racing game, producing new environments shown to be solvable.

limitations: Example data is scarce: MarioGPT trained on 37 levels and LLM Sokoban results scaled with dataset size, so a new game's handful of authored maps may not suffice.
Validity is not guaranteed: about 12% of MarioGPT levels were not completed by an A* agent, so every output needs a solver check.
Conditional control is weak: difficulty conditioning hit its target a third of the time and lowered size and tile-distribution accuracy.
Results are mostly 2D tile grids for small games; large simulation maps with resources, rivers, and settlement suitability carry global constraints these models do not represent.
Training on existing commercial levels such as Super Mario Bros raises IP and platform disclosure questions for shipped use.
mechanism: PCGRL treats level design as a sequential decision problem: an agent edits a tile grid step by step (narrow, turtle, or wide representations of where it may edit) and is rewarded by the change in a quality score such as playability, path length, or region count, so the trained generator builds a level in fast forward passes without example levels. ARLPCG adds a solver agent and rewards the generator for levels that are challenging but solvable, with auxiliary control inputs. Language-model generators serialize levels as text and train or prompt a model to continue them: MarioGPT fine-tunes DistilGPT2 with cross-attention to a prompt naming pipes, enemies, blocks, and elevation; Sokoban generators fine-tune on level corpora; Word2World prompts a general LLM to write a story, extract characters and tiles, and place them. Outputs are checked by search agents or solver bots and rejected or repaired if unplayable. Conditional generators such as EA SEED's match-3 cVAE take size, symmetry, and target difficulty as inputs.
name: Learned level and map generation (PCGRL, MarioGPT, LLM generators)
summary: Generators trained by reinforcement learning or on example levels, including small and large language models that emit tile maps from text prompts, produce playable levels and maps without hand-written generation rules.

affects.note: Motion-matching-quality responsive locomotion fits in a few MB of weights, making it affordable on memory-constrained platforms and for more character types.
Players author new character motions from their own video (inZOI), so the animation set available to life-sim characters is no longer fixed by the studio's mocap library.

key_results.text: Learned motion matching shrank a 590 MB motion matching locomotion system to about 17 MB of weights (8.5 MB with 16-bit quantization), about 70 times smaller, with nearly identical output and constant CPU cost.

FIFA 22's HyperMotion used a machine learning algorithm over more than 8.7 million frames of 22-player match capture to generate player animation in real time, on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Stadia only.
inZOI lets players create character motions by uploading video files, disclosed as an AI-assisted feature.
Unreal Engine ships database motion matching through its Pose Search plugin, the non-learned baseline that learned motion matching compresses.

limitations: Kinematic output ignores physics, so characters still clip or float when the environment differs from the training motion.
Learned motion matching saves memory but not per-character CPU time, which still limits crowd counts.
Video-to-motion quality depends on the uploaded footage; occlusion and camera motion produce artifacts that the game must filter or let players discard.
mechanism: Motion matching picks the next pose by searching a database of mocap frames for the best match to a query of current pose and desired trajectory. Learned motion matching replaces the database with three small networks: a Decompressor that maps a feature vector to a full pose, a Stepper that advances features one frame, and a Projector that maps a query to the nearest valid features, giving nearly identical output at constant CPU cost. HyperMotion trains a model on frames of full-team match capture to generate transitions in real time. Video-to-motion tools estimate 3D poses from ordinary video and retarget them onto a game rig. No physics is simulated.
name: Learned kinematic motion synthesis
summary: Neural networks generate or compress kinematic character animation, as in Ubisoft's learned motion matching, EA's HyperMotion, and inZOI's motion extraction from uploaded video.

affects.note: Voters become LLM agents that hear persuasion from other agents and vote on amendments, as in Project Sid's constitutional votes, instead of computing a vote from satisfaction and bloc membership.
Memes, beliefs, and a seeded religion spread through populations of 500 to one million agents, with content mutating in conversation and spread shaped by social structure or a recommender feed.

Roles emerge from agents' social context and goals (farmers, miners, guards in 30-agent villages) rather than from job slots filled by education level; AgentSociety adds agent-level employment and consumption decisions.
NPC populations can propose, debate, and vote on rule changes in natural language and then comply or not, so legislation is no longer limited to human players in a shared world.

A policy's effect on groups is measured by running it on a population of agents (AgentSociety's universal basic income and hurricane experiments) instead of reading hand-authored weighted edges from policies to voter groups.
Tax compliance becomes an agent decision that responds to law changes and influencer messaging, as in Project Sid's 20% tax experiment, rather than an automatic deduction at the set rate.

A shared world can be populated by hundreds of autonomous agents that keep roles, culture, and rules while human players come and go; PIANO was built for real-time interaction with humans and other agents.
Unplayed households can be advanced by cheap language-agent societies that generate plausible life events instead of fixed event tables.

key_results.text: In Minecraft, PIANO agents in 30-agent villages specialized into persistent roles (farmer, miner, guard, blacksmith) only when the social module was present; agents largely obeyed a 20% tax law and changed compliance after voted constitutional amendments, with pro- and anti-tax influencer agents shifting outcomes; a religion seeded by 20 priests kept spreading through a 500-agent population for two hours.
Project Sid runs above 1,000 agents exceeded Minecraft server limits and agents became sporadically unresponsive, so the main cultural analysis used 500 agents.

AgentSociety simulated over 10,000 agents with about 5 million interactions and reproduced qualitative findings on polarization, inflammatory message spread, universal basic income, and a hurricane shock.
OASIS ran up to one million agents on X- and Reddit-like platforms, replicated information spreading, group polarization, and herd effects, and found stronger group dynamics at larger agent counts.

Concordia formalizes a Game Master entity that grounds natural-language actions in physical, social, or digital space; its 2025 design pattern builds the Game Master from the same components as other entities so designers can configure scenarios without engine code.

limitations: Scale ceilings come from the host game as well as the model: Project Sid agents became unresponsive above 1,000 agents on a Minecraft server.
PIANO agents lack vision and spatial reasoning and have no innate drives such as survival or curiosity, so building and navigation are weak.
Agents built on pretrained models reproduce known human institutions (taxes, votes, religion) rather than inventing new ones, so outcomes are bounded by training data.

Per-agent LLM calls multiply with population; AgentSociety chose an API without request limits to avoid rate-limit artifacts, and none of these papers reports per-agent-hour cost in a form a game could budget against.
Validation is qualitative (matching stylized findings), so designers cannot easily tune or test collective outcomes.
mechanism: Scaling generative agents from tens to thousands needs architecture and infrastructure changes. Project Sid's PIANO runs about ten modules concurrently (memory, action awareness, goal generation, social awareness, talking, skill execution) that read and write a shared agent state; fast modules use small non-LLM models and slow ones call an LLM, and a cognitive controller acts as a bottleneck that broadcasts one high-level decision so speech and actions stay consistent. AgentSociety gives each agent a profile plus emotion, needs, and cognition layers and simulates mobility, social contact, employment, and consumption across linked urban, social, and economic spaces, distributing agents over Ray processes and routing messages over MQTT. Concordia has agents state intended actions in natural language and a Game Master agent decide outcomes. OASIS runs up to one million agents inside a recommender-driven social feed.
name: Many-agent LLM societies
summary: Simulations of hundreds to a million LLM-driven agents with concurrent cognitive modules, shared environments, and message buses that produce role specialization, rule changes, cultural spread, and polarization.

affects.note: Advisors can answer arbitrary player questions about the current situation and recommend actions in context, instead of speaking a fixed catalog of threshold-triggered messages.
The inspection panel can answer why an agent did something by summarizing its needs, itemized mood terms, and recent thought log into a short causal account.
A long nested modifier chain can be condensed into a ranked plain-language list of the largest causes and what would change them, while the numbers still come from the simulation.
Graph changes can be annotated with narrated causes drawn from the event log, such as which policy or disaster preceded a drop.
Recorded events can be retold as biographies, recaps, or highlight summaries for the player, a commentator and reteller role.

key_results.text: Explanations generated from a learned behavior representation plus an LLM were rated about as helpful as a human domain expert's, with little hallucination, and supported clarification and counterfactual follow-ups.
NVIDIA lists a Total War: PHARAOH AI advisor that helps players learn the game's systems using a small on-device model connected to game data; no public release date was found.
SIMA 2 explains its intended steps and answers questions about its behavior and environment in commercial 3D games.
GPT-4 converted 28 players' logs into narrative graphs, letting designers count 53 player-created narrative nodes that their design did not include.

GPT-4 predicted whole text-game state transitions correctly at most 59.9% of the time and environment-driven changes at most 49.7%, so explanations of dynamics must be computed by the simulation and narrated, not inferred by the model.
A 2024 survey found research on LLM commentators and retellers of game events rather limited.

limitations: Wrong but fluent causes: models are unreliable at inferring dynamics, so explanations are only trustworthy when causes are passed in from the simulation.
Serializing large state (thousands of modifiers, long logs) into context is slow and costly; selection of what to include determines what can be explained.
Hard to QA: the answer space is open-ended, and a confident wrong explanation damages trust more than no explanation.
Shipped evidence is thin: known game examples are tech demos or research previews.
mechanism: The game serializes the relevant slice of state (indicator values and their contributing modifiers, an agent's thought log and action trace, recent events) into the prompt, or exposes it through retrieval or tool calls over game data and documentation, and the model answers a player question or writes a summary. Zhang et al. first learn a compact representation of an agent's behavior from observed states and actions, then have the LLM explain from that representation, which limits hallucination and supports follow-up and what-if questions. For designers, a model can segment play logs into strategies and merge them into a graph to compare with the intended path. The explanation layer reads state and does not write it, so the simulation stays deterministic.
name: LLM explanation of simulation state
summary: Language models that read simulation state, modifier breakdowns, agent traces, or event logs and answer why and what-if questions or summarize what happened for players and designers.

affects.note: The director can author an event in language for the exact current state, check it against canon and rules, and narrate it, instead of choosing among a finite catalog of pre-written incidents by a pacing budget.
