Follow-up beats are generated from story state and player intent rather than scheduled by authored templates with trigger predicates, while the player still experiences multi-step chains.

Characters can ask for things tied to the specific story so far, not only fetch templates with filled slots; ungrounded models invent quests that do not exist, so requests must be checked against state.
Story continuation from Do, Say, Story, and See inputs makes the whole narrative generated content; grounded engines turn it into typed state changes.

Any typed action is adjudicated for plausibility and consequence rather than matched against a parser's verb list, so unanticipated approaches produce new narrative paths (53 emergent nodes in one 28-player study).
NPCs with backstories, goals, and personality are generated from designer criteria and voiced in dialogue, removing per-character writing.

claims.text: Steam requires games with live-generated AI content to disclose it and describe guardrails against illegal output, and does not permit live-generated adult sexual content.
Dungeon Masters using CALYPSO presented some generated text almost directly and treated rougher output as ideas while keeping creative control.

PANGeA generated settings, key items, and Big Five personality-biased NPCs from designer criteria and used the model to keep free-text player input within the narrative, tested in a browser demo and a Unity game.

Steam generative AI disclosures rose from about 1,000 games in April 2024 to 7,818 (about 7% of the catalog, a little under 20% of 2025 releases) in July 2025 and 10,258 (about 8%) in November 2025; about 60% of disclosures concern visual assets, so live-generated runtime systems such as LLM narration are a small share.

key_results.text: AI Dungeon 2 (December 2019) ran the full 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 and moved to GPT-3 in mid-2020, reaching over 100,000 players in its first week and 1.5 million by June 2020.

AI Dungeon's 2021 content filter, added to block sexual content involving minors, produced false positives on innocuous text and led human moderators to read flagged private stories, prompting review bombing.

In a 28-player study with five GPT-4 NPCs holding backstories, clues, and ordered goals, play produced 53 narrative nodes absent from the designers' graph; about 15 seconds of lag frustrated 40% of players and NPCs forgot earlier statements in 10% of reports.

Hidden Door announced early access in August 2025 and offers licensed worlds such as Dracula; its engine checks every story turn against canon and rules before display and reports a tuned 1.7B model beating a 120B general model on one core task.

Concordia's Game Master converts agents' natural-language actions into outcomes and checks physical plausibility, and its 2025 design pattern classifies uses as Simulationist, Dramatist, or Evaluationist.
Surveyed LLM game masters tend to accommodate even bizarre player requests that human GMs would curb, and LLM NPCs can invent quests that do not exist in the game.

limitations: Long-session consistency: models forget or contradict earlier facts unless state is externalized into memory or a typed world model.
Accommodation bias: models rarely say no, which removes challenge and lets players talk past any obstacle.
Content moderation is hard: AI Dungeon's filter both missed and over-blocked, and Steam requires guardrail disclosure for live-generated content.
Latency of several to 15 seconds per turn frustrated players in a GPT-4 study; multi-step grounded pipelines add calls per turn.
Every turn is an inference cost for the life of the service, which pushes products to subscriptions or small tuned models.
mechanism: The player types an intent; the system assembles a prompt from recent story, pinned memories, and setting notes and asks the model to continue the story, as AI Dungeon has since 2019. Grounded variants split the job: actors state intended actions in language, a Game Master component checks plausibility against rules and state, decides what happens, writes state changes, and only then narrates (Concordia). Hidden Door runs intent through plan, canon check, and world-state update steps over a typed, auditable world model, using many small tuned models for about 100 narrative tasks; its example blocks Dracula from entering a house uninvited. Research systems generate setting, items, and NPCs from designer criteria and use the model to validate free-text input against the story (PANGeA), or assist a human Dungeon Master (CALYPSO).
name: LLM game master and narrative director
summary: A language model that adjudicates player and NPC intentions, decides outcomes, generates events and quests, and narrates them, either free-form or checked against a typed world state and canon.

affects.note: The recipe space becomes unbounded: any pair of items yields a generated result rather than a lookup in a finite designer table, and the first answer is cached as the permanent recipe.

Interactions between arbitrary materials or elements can be resolved by a model rather than an authored pair table, but whole-state accuracy near 60% means results must be bounded to simple outputs and cached.
Generated results are written back as shared, persistent rules rather than one-off text, so the world's content grows with play and stays consistent across players.
Collections become open-ended races to discover never-generated items, with a First Discovery credit for the first player to create each one.
A language model decides the result of each new combination and caches it, turning a finite authored recipe graph into an open one (Infinite Craft).

key_results.text: Infinite Craft (January 2024) starts from water, fire, wind, and earth and generates a new element and emoji with Llama 2 and Llama 3.1 for any untried pair, storing the result so each pair gives every player the same answer; traffic reached hundreds of millions of recipes a day.

On 76,369 transitions from 31 text games, GPT-4 predicted the full next state correctly at most 59.9% of the time, up to 77.1% for action-driven and at most 49.7% for environment-driven changes; humans scored about 80% on a subset where GPT-4 scored about 50%.
Concordia's Game Master uses a language model to decide whether stated actions are physically plausible and what their effects are.

limitations: Accuracy: as a general state simulator GPT-4 is right on whole-state transitions at most 59.9% of the time, so errors compound over multi-step dynamics.
Legibility: generated rules follow word association rather than a learnable system, so players cannot predict outcomes from principles.
Cost and load scale with unique queries; Infinite Craft's traffic overloaded its servers.
Outputs must be filtered for offensive results because every cached answer becomes permanent shared content.
mechanism: The game describes the inputs (two items, or an object state plus an action) as text and asks the model for the result, constrained to a short name, an icon, or a small state diff. Infinite Craft first looks the pair up in a database; only a never-tried pair goes to the model (Llama 2, later Llama 3.1), and the answer is stored, so the rule becomes fixed and shared by all players after the first query and the first finder is credited. The cache turns a stochastic model into a growing deterministic rule table and bounds cost to unique queries. Benchmarks of LLMs as text world simulators measure how often the predicted next state matches the true one.
name: LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic)
summary: A language model computes the outcome of an interaction (two elements combined, an action on an object) from a text description of the inputs, with results cached so every player sees the same rule.

affects.note: Batched GPU rigid-body solvers step thousands of worlds or bodies per kernel launch, so physics-heavy evaluation that was CPU-bound becomes cheap enough for large sweeps.
Locomotion policies train in seconds to minutes on one GPU (Brax, MuJoCo Playground), so a creature could learn to move or act through RL during a play session instead of from canned animation.

A player-built creature or machine can be dropped into thousands of parallel worlds and have a controller trained for its specific body, so assembled designs move competently without the player programming them.
Fitness can be measured by simulating every individual of a large population in its own physics world each generation, so selection acts on actual behavior rather than on summed stat values.
A player design can be scored over hundreds of randomized loads, terrains or seeds in parallel, giving a robustness distribution instead of one deterministic test run.
Millions of simulated matches per hour let designers check how attribute weights and tactic modifiers shift outcome distributions before shipping a match-engine change.
GPUDrive shows multi-agent vehicle simulation above one million steps per second, which points to agent-level traffic at counts where city builders now fall back to aggregate flow.
Cheap batched rollouts make it practical to search utility-curve weights, or train a policy to replace them, against metrics such as survival or need satisfaction over many simulated colonies.

key_results.text: Isaac Gym ran physics and policy training on a single GPU and reported 2-3 orders of magnitude faster RL training than pipelines using a CPU simulator.

Brax reported millions of simulation steps per second on one accelerator and hundreds of millions across accelerators, training Ant locomotion in about ten seconds versus close to half an hour for standard PPO.

Madrona's GPU batch ECS ran OpenAI Hide and Seek at over 1.9 million steps per second, Overcooked-AI at 40 million and Hanabi at 20 million on an RTX 4090, 5-33x faster than strong 32-thread CPU baselines.
Craftax reimplemented the survival-crafting game Crafter in JAX, ran up to 250x faster than the Python original, and trained PPO for 1 billion interactions in under an hour on one GPU.
GPUDrive, built on Madrona, simulated multi-agent driving from real road scenarios at over one million steps per second.
MuJoCo Playground (2025) trained locomotion and manipulation policies in minutes on a single GPU and transferred them zero-shot to real robots.
Genesis (December 2024) was publicized as reaching 43 million FPS (430,000x real time) on simple scenes; press noted skepticism and that contact-rich dexterous scenes remain hard.

GPU physics became more open in 2025: NVIDIA released PhysX 5.6 GPU source under BSD-3 in April, and the Warp-based Newton engine (NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Disney Research) moved to the Linux Foundation in September.

limitations: Speedups come from running many independent worlds in parallel; a single large coupled world, such as one city, gains much less and per-world latency does not improve.
Game logic must be rewritten in a GPU-friendly form (JAX in Craftax, C++ compiled to CUDA in GPUDrive and Madrona), which is a port rather than a recompile.
Madrona requires all component archetypes to be declared up front and does not support adding or removing components at runtime; it is labeled research code with breaking API changes.
Headline frame rates are for simple scenes; contact-rich and dexterous scenes remain hard and much slower (reported caveat on Genesis).
Much of the stack is NVIDIA-specific: MuJoCo Warp needs an NVIDIA GPU for speed, and porting PhysX's 500+ CUDA kernels to other vendors is described as a lot of work.
Policies trained in a batched simulator exploit its physics quirks, so behavior must be re-validated in the shipping engine if that engine differs.
mechanism: World state for N independent instances is stored as structure-of-arrays tensors in accelerator memory. Each tick launches one set of kernels that integrates physics, evaluates game logic, and computes observations and rewards for every instance at once, so policy inference and training read the state without CPU-GPU copies. Implementations compile the step function: JAX/XLA (Brax, MJX, Craftax), CUDA kernels written in Python (NVIDIA Warp, MuJoCo Warp), or a GPU entity-component-system with a task graph (Madrona, where game logic is C++ compiled to CUDA). Throughput comes from parallelism across worlds, not from making one world faster, so the main uses are reinforcement learning (billions of steps), parameter sweeps, and evaluating many randomized variants of one design.
name: Massively parallel GPU simulation
summary: Simulators that keep thousands of world instances as tensors on a GPU or TPU and step them all in one kernel, raising throughput to millions of steps per second for agent training and Monte Carlo sweeps.

affects.note: Trip routing changes from each agent reacting to current travel times, which oscillates, to an equilibrium in which drivers anticipate congestion, computed once for the population at a cost independent of car count.
Park visitors can choose attractions in equilibrium with expected queues and crowding rather than greedily, producing realistic spreading of crowds across a park.
Queue choice and arrival timing become equilibrium behavior, so changing capacity at one service shifts load across the others as people anticipate the change.
Prices can come from many small rational producers and consumers in equilibrium (as in MFG models of energy markets), instead of a fixed elasticity formula.
One equilibrium policy over positions serves any number of agents, like a flow field that already includes congestion effects, replacing per-agent searches.
Mode split solved as a population equilibrium in which each traveler responds to congestion created by everyone else.

key_results.text: Lasry and Lions (2007) formulated mean field games as coupled forward-backward nonlinear PDEs for many rational players reacting to aggregates and showed the problems are generally well-posed.
Online mirror descent converged to MFG Nash equilibria under monotonicity, outperformed fictitious play, and solved MFGs with hundreds of billions of states.
Mean-field MARL let each agent learn against its neighbors' mean action, scaling multi-agent learning to many-agent battle games and solving the Ising model with model-free RL.
MFGs are applied to energy markets, bitcoin mining, macro-finance models and contract theory.
Learning methods for static, stationary and evolutive MFG equilibria and social optima are now surveyed as an established toolkit.

limitations: Assumes anonymous, symmetric, individually negligible agents; named characters with unique state, or a player large enough to move the aggregate, need major-player extensions.
Equilibrium describes settled behavior; the learning, overshoot and panic dynamics games often want are absent unless modeled separately.
The forward-backward coupling needs the whole horizon at once, so player interventions mid-run require re-solving or a fast approximate solver.
Convergence guarantees such as those for online mirror descent need monotonicity assumptions that game rules can violate.
No game implementation was found in this run's sources.
mechanism: Each agent is small, anonymous and interchangeable, so the game depends on others only through the population distribution m(t,x). An equilibrium is a fixed point: the representative agent's value function u solves a backward Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation given m, and m evolves forward by a Fokker-Planck equation under the resulting policy. Numerical and learning methods iterate this pair: fictitious play averages past best responses; online mirror descent accumulates Q-values and updates the policy by a softmax of them; RL variants learn from samples when the model is unknown. Mean-field multi-agent RL applies the same idea locally, with each agent learning against the mean action of its neighbors. Cost scales with the size of the individual state space, not with the number of agents.
name: Mean field games and mean-field learning
summary: Mean field game theory replaces an N-player game with one representative agent responding to the population distribution, and recent learning methods compute these equilibria for state spaces of hundreds of billions of states.

affects.note: Weather becomes a coherent global field with fronts, cyclones and multi-day evolution across hundreds of variables, instead of a per-region Markov chain of weather states.
Ensembles (50 GenCast members) give calibrated probabilities, so an in-game forecast can carry real uncertainty that players plan against and that occasionally misses honestly.
Storms emerge from atmospheric state with forecastable tracks (Aurora beat operational centres on 5-day cyclone tracks), turning disasters from dice rolls into threats with lead time.
Aurora's fine-tuned air-quality forecasts run about 100,000x faster than CAMS, a path to pollution plumes transported by simulated wind at playable cost.
Earth-system foundation models fine-tuned to several domains suggest climate sims coupling atmosphere, ocean waves and air chemistry, though they are trained for days-ahead weather, not decades.

key_results.text: GraphCast produced 0.25 degree, 10-day global forecasts in under one minute on one TPU v4 machine and beat ECMWF HRES on over 90% of 1,380 verification targets.
GenCast's 50-member diffusion ensembles were more skillful than ECMWF's ENS on 97.2% of 1,320 targets; one 15-day forecast took about 8 minutes on a Cloud TPU v5.

Aurora (1.3B parameters) matched or beat operational systems on 74% of air-quality targets, 86% of ocean-wave variables and 92% of 0.1 degree weather targets, beat seven centres on 5-day cyclone tracks, and ran about 100,000x faster than CAMS for air quality.
ECMWF made its AIFS machine-learned model operational on 25 February 2025, reporting about 1,000x less energy per forecast than its physics model, at 28 km grid spacing versus 9 km.
FGN (2025) reported state-of-the-art ensemble skill and cyclone tracks while being trained only on per-location targets.

limitations: Trained on Earth's reanalysis record, so they reproduce Earth's atmosphere only; fictional planets, altered geography or deliberate climate change lie outside the training data.
Grids are coarse for game maps: 0.25 degree (about 28 km at the equator), and operational AIFS runs at 28 km.
Inference needs an accelerator and gigabytes of weights (Aurora has 1.3B parameters), heavy for client-side use.
Designers cannot author dramatic timing; the model follows the statistics of real weather, so pacing must be imposed by selecting or conditioning forecasts.
Autoregressive rollouts are validated to 10-15 days; behavior over seasons or years is not established by these sources.
mechanism: Models take the current and recent atmospheric state on a global 0.25 degree latitude-longitude grid (temperature, wind, humidity, pressure at many levels plus surface variables) and predict the state one fixed step later; rolling the prediction forward gives a 10-15 day forecast. GraphCast maps grid cells onto a multi-resolution icosahedral mesh and runs learned message passing there. GenCast is a conditional diffusion model that samples stochastic trajectories in 12-hour steps, so repeated samples form an ensemble with calibrated spread. FGN (2025) builds ensembles from learned model perturbations trained on CRPS. Aurora is a 1.3B-parameter foundation model pretrained on over a million hours of geophysical data and fine-tuned for air quality, ocean waves, cyclone tracks and 0.1 degree weather. Inference replaces hours on a supercomputer with seconds to minutes on one accelerator.
name: Machine-learned weather forecasting
summary: Neural networks trained on decades of atmospheric reanalysis forecast global weather 10-15 days ahead in seconds to minutes on one accelerator, matching or beating physics-based operational models on most verification targets.

affects.note: Competitor AI becomes a policy trained by self-play against the game's own rules, so it re-adapts when economic rules change in a patch instead of needing rewritten heuristics; training compute per rule set is the cost.
Self-play agents trained on each candidate tree reveal dominant research orders and unused branches, the same comparison AlphaZero made across chess rule variants.
Each toggle combination is a rule variant; converged self-play under each variant measures how much a policy shifts outcomes and flags toggles that are strictly dominant or never worth enacting.

Sample-efficient model-based learners (EfficientZero needed about two hours of experience) make it plausible for a creature to learn new behaviors from player reward within a session, by planning in a learned model of its world rather than reacting with a fixed network.

Opponents plan with a learned value function plus search over unit actions, giving strong play in operational simulations where hand-written doctrine is brittle; latent models allow planning where exact rollouts are too slow.

key_results.text: AlphaZero reached superhuman chess, shogi, and Go within 24 hours from random play given only the rules, beating a world-champion program in each game.
MuZero matched AlphaZero in Go, chess, and shogi and surpassed R2D2 on Atari while learning its own model instead of being given the rules (Nature, December 2020).
MuZero's board-game training used 16 TPUs for training and 1,000 for self-play at 800 simulations per move, and it performed poorly on 6 Atari games.
EfficientZero reached 194.3% mean and 109.0% median human-normalized score on Atari 100k from about two hours of real-time game experience.
AlphaZero trained from scratch on nine chess rule variants was used to compare decisiveness, piece values, and dynamism across variants as an in silico game balance assessment.

DreamerV3 (Nature, April 2025) beat specialized methods on over 150 tasks with one configuration and was the first algorithm to collect Minecraft diamonds from scratch without human data, first at about 30M environment steps (about 17 days of play).

Dreamer 4 (September 2025) learned a Minecraft world model that runs interactively on one GPU and obtained diamonds from offline data only, choosing sequences of over 20,000 keyboard and mouse actions from pixels.
MuZero-RC chose per-frame VP9 quantisation on part of YouTube live traffic for an average 4% bitrate reduction, its first production deployment, outside games.

limitations: Training is expensive: MuZero's board-game runs used 16 TPUs for training and 1,000 for self-play, and each significant rule change needs retraining or fine-tuning.
Self-play converges to strong play, not human play, so balance conclusions can reflect exploits humans would never find or use.
Learned dynamics drift over long rollouts; MuZero did poorly on 6 Atari games and DreamerV3 needed about 30M steps (17 days of play) for its first Minecraft diamond.
Most simulation games are many-player, simultaneous-move, partly hidden, and long-horizon, which the two-player perfect-information AlphaZero setup does not cover directly.
Policies are opaque, so designers cannot read why an AI rival chose a strategy, and giving it a personality requires reward shaping rather than editing rules.
mechanism: AlphaZero pairs MCTS with a network that outputs a move prior p and a value v for a state; games generated by the search train p toward search visit counts and v toward outcomes, so search and network improve each other given only the rules. MuZero drops the need for rules at planning time: a representation network encodes observations into a latent state, a dynamics network predicts the next latent state and reward for an action, and a prediction network outputs policy and value, so MCTS runs entirely in the learned latent space. EfficientZero adds self-supervised consistency and value-prefix losses for sample efficiency. Dreamer learns a recurrent world model and trains an actor-critic on imagined trajectories; DreamerV3 adds symlog and return normalization so one hyperparameter set works across domains, and Dreamer 4 trains its world model mostly on unlabeled video and learns the policy offline inside it. For design work the same loop can be retrained on each rule variant and the converged play compared.
name: Self-play planning with learned models (AlphaZero, MuZero, Dreamer)
summary: Agents that combine tree search or imagined rollouts with neural policy and value networks trained by self-play, where MuZero and Dreamer also learn the environment's dynamics, reach superhuman play from rules or pixels alone.

affects.note: Agents choose actions by sampling futures from the game's forward model and backing up outcomes, instead of scoring one-step options with hand-tuned utility curves, so choices account for consequences several actions ahead at a per-decision compute cost.

Tactical AI plans multi-unit action sequences within a time budget, as in Fable Legends' real-time tactical planning, rather than following scripted doctrine; the iteration budget becomes a difficulty lever.

AI factions can weigh war, peace, and alliance options by simulating future turns of the campaign, the kind of high-level campaign decision Total War: Rome II gave to MCTS, so choices respond to the actual strategic position instead of fixed opinion thresholds.

AI competitors can pick prices, expansions, and acquisitions by rolling the economic model forward, so rival play adapts to the player's position and to rule changes without bespoke heuristics per market rule.
Governors or managers given a subsystem can search over action sequences toward the player-set goal with the same forward model, staying competent in rule configurations designers did not script for.

key_results.text: Kocsis and Szepesvari introduced UCT, applying the UCB1 bandit rule to node selection in Monte Carlo planning (ECML 2006); Coulom coined the name Monte Carlo tree search the same year.
A 2012 survey in IEEE TCIAIG catalogued MCTS variants, enhancements, and applications in board, card, and video games after its first six years.
Total War: Rome II used MCTS in its high-level campaign AI, and Fable Legends used real-time MCTS for tactical planning (2015 talk).

limitations: Needs a fast, copyable forward model; a full simulation state with thousands of agents is expensive to clone and step, so practical use usually requires an abstracted model or macro-actions.
Random playouts estimate value poorly in long-horizon systems with delayed consequences such as economies and colony survival unless a heuristic rollout policy or evaluation function is supplied.
Time-budgeted search returns different moves on different hardware, which breaks replays and lockstep multiplayer unless budgets are counted in iterations with seeded randomness.
Determinized search over hidden information averages over sampled worlds and can make choices that are only good if it could see the hidden state (strategy fusion).
mechanism: Each iteration has four steps. Selection descends from the root by a tree policy; UCT picks the child that maximizes mean reward plus c*sqrt(ln N / n), trading exploitation against exploration. Expansion adds an untried child. Simulation plays forward from that node with a cheap default policy (random or heuristic) to a terminal state or depth limit. Backpropagation adds the outcome to the visit count and value of every node on the path. The search is anytime: it stops after an iteration count or time budget and returns the most-visited action. It needs only a forward model that can copy a state, list legal actions, and apply them, so it works for rule sets without a known evaluation function. Variants add chance nodes, determinization or information-set trees for hidden information, simultaneous moves, and macro-actions that search over plans instead of single moves.
name: Monte Carlo tree search for game AI
summary: A best-first search that grows a game tree from repeated simulated playouts and picks branches with a bandit rule such as UCT, letting AI players plan from a forward model without a hand-tuned evaluation function.

affects.note: In WHAMM the avatar's movement and camera are rendered by the model from controller input, at 10+ fps with a 0.9 second context.

Movement and collisions follow learned game dynamics; the Nature paper's consistency criterion is that generated play respects controller input and the game's physics, which is measured statistically rather than enforced.
Designers insert an object or character into a frame and the model generates plausible gameplay around it (persistency), giving a preview of how a content change might play before it is built.

key_results.text: The Nature paper (February 2025) frames consistency, diversity, and persistency of user modifications as the three capabilities generative models need to support game ideation, and shows WHAM provides them.

WHAM was trained on more than 1 billion images and controller actions, over 7 years of continuous play, from Bleeding Edge matches recorded under the game's EULA; model weights, sample data, and the WHAM Demonstrator were released on Azure AI Foundry.

WHAMM ran a playable section of one Quake II level at 10+ fps and 640x360 after training on one week of gameplay data; enemies were blurry, damage could be wrong, context was 0.9 seconds, and health counters were unreliable.

limitations: WHAM-1.6B generates about one image per second at 300x180, too slow and too small for play; WHAMM trades data scope (one level section) for speed.
Needs years of recorded human play with consent terms for a single game; few studios hold such datasets.
Context of under a second (WHAMM) means objects out of view are forgotten.
Counts, damage, and other exact quantities are unreliable in generated frames.
mechanism: Frames are encoded into discrete image tokens and controller inputs into action tokens; a decoder-only transformer models the interleaved sequence, so it predicts both how the world evolves and what a human player is likely to do next. Prompting with a few frames yields many plausible continuations (diversity); a designer can edit a frame, such as inserting a character, and the model carries the edit forward (persistency). WHAM-1.6B produces about one frame per second at 300x180. WHAMM replaces token-by-token decoding with MaskGIT-style parallel prediction (a 500M backbone plus a 250M refiner) to reach more than 10 fps at 640x360 on Quake II.
name: Muse World and Human Action Model (WHAM)
summary: Microsoft Research's WHAM is a transformer trained on seven years of Bleeding Edge play that generates both future frames and the player's controller actions, aimed at gameplay ideation, with a real-time Quake II follow-up (WHAMM).

affects.note: Local per-cell material rules can be learned from examples of desired behavior instead of hand-coded; DiffLogic CA recovered Game of Life exactly as a compact logic circuit cheap enough for per-pixel use.
Regenerating NCA regrow damaged shapes and 3D NCA regrow parts of machines, enabling destructible structures and organisms that heal from local rules rather than respawning.
A seed block placed by the player can grow into a castle or tree over time under a learned 3D rule, a growth-based alternative to instant procedural detailing.
Tile maps and levels can be grown by NCA generators selected by quality-diversity search for solvability and diversity, replacing hand-tuned noise and placement rules.

key_results.text: Growing NCA grew an image from one seed cell with a shared update network of about 8,000 parameters; models trained on damaged samples regrew erased regions, including damage types not seen in training.
NCA texture models with 5,868 parameters synthesized textures interactively in real time in a WebGL demo.
3D NCA grew Minecraft castles, apartment blocks and trees, some over 3,000 blocks, and regrew parts of simple functional machines.
Quality-diversity search (CMA-ME) produced diverse NCA level generators for maze, Sokoban and Zelda domains, often meeting solvability criteria, and explored level space better than a CPPN baseline.

DiffLogic CA (2025) learned Conway's Game of Life from all 512 3x3 configurations as a 336-gate binary circuit and grew patterns such as a lizard with 577 gates, with asynchronous and self-healing variants.

limitations: Each trained rule targets one pattern, texture or structure family; changing the target requires retraining.
Growth unfolds over many steps, so getting a stable result has a latency that instant procedural methods do not have.
Learned rules are opaque to designers and players, apart from small logic-gate circuits, which makes failures hard to diagnose.
Demonstrations are small 2D images, 3D structures of a few thousand blocks, and simple tile domains; robustness under player interference at game scale is not shown.
mechanism: Each grid cell holds a state vector (16 channels in Growing NCA: RGB, an alpha channel that marks living cells, and hidden signaling channels). Every step a cell perceives its 3x3 neighborhood through fixed Sobel gradient filters, a shared network of about 8,000 parameters maps the perception vector to a state increment, and a random mask applies the update to roughly half the cells, so no global clock is needed. Cells with no living neighbor are zeroed. The rule is trained by backpropagating through many steps toward a target image or style, with damaged samples in the training pool to teach regeneration. Variants use 3D convolutions for voxel structures, quality-diversity search instead of gradients for game levels, or differentiable logic gates that compile to a discrete binary circuit (DiffLogic CA).
name: Neural cellular automata
summary: Cellular automata whose local update rule is a small learned network or logic circuit, trained so that cells grow, maintain, and regenerate a target pattern, texture, structure, or level from a seed.

affects.note: Upscaling and frame generation raise displayed frame rates in GPU-heavy flight and driving sims for the same render cost; generated frames do not sample new input, so frame generation adds latency that hurts precise hand-flying or driving.

Neural denoising and the neural radiance cache make dynamic multi-bounce lighting affordable, so player-built interiors and towns can be lit correctly across a full diurnal cycle where baked lighting cannot follow player construction.

Up to 7x VRAM savings from neural texture compression and cheaper layered materials let more distinct high-detail decor assets be resident at once, raising the variety a beauty-driven builder can show on screen.

key_results.text: DLSS 4 (January 2025) introduced Multi Frame Generation of up to three extra frames per rendered frame on RTX 50 GPUs and transformer models for super resolution and ray reconstruction, with 75 games and apps at launch and up to 8x frame rate over brute-force rendering.

RTX neural shaders (January 2025) included neural texture compression using up to 7x less VRAM than block-compressed textures at equal quality, neural materials up to 5x faster, and a neural radiance cache for multi-bounce indirect lighting, with DirectX cooperative vector support announced.
By January 2026 over 250 titles supported Multi Frame Generation and over 400 games and apps supported DLSS Super Resolution; DLSS 4.5 added a 6X mode generating up to five frames per rendered frame.

DLSS 5 launched on 2026-09-03 in NBA 2K27 as a deterministic one-frame-in, one-frame-out neural pass that adds lighting and material detail, with structure and tone intensity controls and semantic masks for developers.

DLSS 5's reveal drew largely negative reaction from players and developers over altered faces and art direction, and a reported 50 to 60 percent frame-rate cost; frame generation in general adds input latency and can introduce artifacts.
Simulation titles use DLSS: Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) supports DLSS upscaling and DLSS Frame Generation, and Cities: Skylines II supports DLSS upscaling.

limitations: Changes presentation, not simulation: CPU-bound simulation games (agent counts, pathfinding, economy ticks) gain nothing from GPU-side neural rendering.
Frame generation adds input latency and artifacts; DLSS 5's final pass reportedly costs 50 to 60 percent of frame rate and can alter art direction.
Hardware-gated: Multi Frame Generation and DLSS 5 require RTX 50-series GPUs at launch, and neural shader features depend on vendor SDKs and cooperative vector support.
mechanism: DLSS Super Resolution reconstructs a high-resolution frame from a lower-resolution render plus motion vectors with a transformer network (from DLSS 4); Multi Frame Generation predicts up to three (DLSS 4) or five (DLSS 4.5) frames between rendered frames; Ray Reconstruction replaces hand-tuned denoisers. Neural shaders embed small MLPs inside shader code and run them on tensor units: neural texture compression decodes textures from learned latents, neural materials evaluate layered BRDFs, and the neural radiance cache learns multi-bounce indirect light online. DirectX cooperative vectors expose this to cross-vendor shaders. DLSS 5 adds a final network pass that adds lighting and material detail from color and motion vectors, with developer intensity controls and masks.
name: Neural rendering in the graphics pipeline
summary: Small neural networks inside the renderer upscale frames, generate extra frames, denoise ray tracing, decode compressed textures and layered materials, and since DLSS 5 re-light the final frame, all without touching simulation state.

affects.note: Free-text and voice input to characters runs on the player's GPU, removing per-token server cost and network round trips, so open conversation can be offered to every player of a premium game.
Smart Zois pick actions with a small model that reads needs, surroundings, and inner thoughts rather than only scored need curves, while the game's action set stays the same.
Characters generate text thoughts about events and reflect on past decisions, giving each agent a running inner monologue rather than a list of authored mood modifiers.
Total War: PHARAOH's ACE advisor answers questions about the game's systems from a small on-device model connected to game data, instead of firing authored lines when indicators cross thresholds.
A co-playable teammate such as PUBG Ally takes spoken orders about movement, looting, and strategy mid-match and acts on them, a command channel that needs no menus or ping wheel.

key_results.text: Minitron pruning and distillation compressed Mistral NeMo 12B to an 8B model and Llama 3.1 8B to 4B, and NVIDIA's ACE character stack lists Minitron 8B, 4B, and 2B instruct models, the 2B fitting in about 1.5 GB of VRAM.
GPTQ quantizes weights to 3-4 bits with minimal accuracy loss and generates 3.25-4.5x faster than FP16; AWQ's 4-bit runtime is over 3x faster than FP16 on desktop and mobile GPUs.

inZOI (early access March 2025) ships an on-device SLM through which typed prompts influence Zois' actions and thoughts; an August 2025 update made Smart Zois observe surroundings and react to events better and align actions with inner thoughts.

KRAFTON ran a public PUBG Ally beta (Ally Duo, 17 June to 1 July 2026) in which an AI teammate takes voice instructions via an on-device small language model built on NVIDIA ACE with speech-to-text and text-to-speech.
NVIDIA's in-game inference SDK requires an RTX 30-series class GPU or newer with at least 8 GB of VRAM (12 GB recommended), and some plugins need RTX 40-series.
Hidden Door reports that a 1.7B model tuned on real play beat a 120B general model on one of its core narrative tasks.

limitations: Hardware floor: the inference SDK needs an RTX 30-series class GPU with 8 GB of VRAM minimum, which excludes many players and consoles, and the model competes with rendering for VRAM and GPU time.
Small models are less capable at multi-step reasoning, so vendors offload strategic planning to cloud models, reintroducing cost and latency.
Quality and safety filters must also run locally; local weights can be extracted or modified by players.
Player reception risk: inZOI drew negative user reviews in May 2025 after Krafton announced its generative AI use.
Exact model sizes and latency in shipped titles are mostly undisclosed.
mechanism: A 12B or 8B model is pruned in depth and width and distilled into an 8B, 4B, or 2B student (Minitron), then weights are quantized to 3-4 bits with second-order (GPTQ) or activation-aware (AWQ) methods, shrinking memory so a 2B model fits in about 1.5 GB of VRAM. An in-game inference SDK runs the models in-process and schedules them alongside graphics on the same GPU. A character loop chains on-device speech recognition, the small model (perceive, decide, act, reflect), text-to-speech, and facial animation, with an in-process embedding model for memory retrieval; slow strategic planning can be offloaded to a larger cloud model while fast decisions stay local. Fine-tuning a small model on a narrow game task can beat much larger general models on that task.
name: On-device small language models for characters
summary: Pruned, distilled, and 4-bit quantized language, speech, and embedding models that run on the player's GPU beside rendering to drive character decisions, dialogue, and voice without per-token server cost.

affects.note: Objectives stop being a fixed authored list: a model writes each task and its success check as code, admitted only if it is neither already solved nor out of reach, so a sandbox can keep issuing new challenges.

Terrain parameters are mutated against measured agent or player performance, as POET did with walker terrain roughness, gaps, and stumps, so maps grow harder along the axes a player has already mastered.
Challenge scales with measured learning progress per task family rather than with wealth or time survived, using a band that admits only tasks the current agent or player can partly solve.
A creature or companion can improve through self-proposed practice tasks with model-estimated rewards, the loop SIMA 2 used, rather than only through explicit player reward and punishment.
Requests can be generated beyond fixed templates, with completion conditions written as generated code over simulation state and an archive of past requests used to avoid repeats.

key_results.text: POET (2019) co-generated environment challenges and agents, producing behaviors that solved challenges direct optimization and a direct-path curriculum could not, and transfer between environments was essential.
Enhanced POET (2020) added a domain-general measure of meaningful novelty, an efficient transfer heuristic, a more flexible environment encoding, and a measure of ongoing open-ended innovation.

OMNI-EPIC (2024) used foundation models to write environment and reward code for tasks judged both learnable and interesting, kept proposing new tasks, and adjusted difficulty to the agent's learning progress.

SIMA 2 (November 2025) learned new games through self-directed play from Gemini-proposed tasks and estimated rewards without new human data, improved on previously failed tasks across generations including in Genie 3 worlds, and remained a limited research preview.

limitations: Cost is dominated by training or evaluating an agent on every candidate task, so the loop runs offline and is too slow to respond to a live player directly.
Interestingness and success are judged by foundation models or generated code that can be wrong, and generated reward code can be satisfied by unintended behavior.
SIMA 2 still struggles with very long-horizon tasks, short memory, precise low-level control, and robust visual understanding, which limits the tasks it can practice.
Worlds generated by video world models are approximate and short-horizon rather than rules-exact simulations, so success checks inside them are approximate.
mechanism: POET keeps a population of environment-agent pairs. It mutates environment parameters (for a 2D walker: roughness, gap width, stump height), admits a child environment only if current agents score within a band that is neither too easy nor too hard, optimizes each agent in its paired environment, and periodically tests whether an agent from another pair does better there, transferring it if so. Enhanced POET adds a novelty measure based on how agents rank on an environment and a more flexible environment encoding. OMNI-EPIC replaces parameter mutation with a foundation model that writes environment and reward code for a physics simulator, conditioned on an archive of solved and failed tasks; a model of interestingness rejects near-duplicates, an RL agent trains on each task, and a success check decides whether the task enters the archive. SIMA 2 has Gemini propose tasks and estimate rewards in commercial games and in Genie 3 generated worlds, then trains later agents on its own experience. The shared loop is: generate a task, check it is learnable, train, archive, repeat.
name: Open-ended co-generation of environments and agents
summary: Systems that keep generating new environments or tasks at the edge of an agent's ability and train agents on them, from POET's co-evolved terrains to OMNI-EPIC's foundation-model-written task code and SIMA 2 practicing in Genie 3 worlds.

affects.note: Matrix-Game 2.0 was fine-tuned on 574 hours of GTA driving; car handling is reproduced from video rather than tire and suspension models, with no guarantee of consistent grip or mass.
Walking, turning, and jumping are rendered from a unified camera-action space; GameCraft's action space lacks shooting, throwing, and explosions.

A world starts from any image, sketch, or photo (Mirage 2, GameCraft); pose-indexed memory in Matrix-Game 3.0 and WorldPlay lets revisited areas stay consistent for about a minute, still far short of a save file.
Typed text during play adds or restyles objects and scenes (Yan editing, Mirage 2 commands, Odyssey-2 prompts), so content is requested at runtime rather than authored.
Mirage 2 lets players save and share generated worlds; what is shared is a prompt and seed image for a model rather than an asset bundle, so the receiver needs the same hosted model.
Contact and motion responses come from video priors; out-of-domain views degrade (Matrix-Game 2.0 reports over-saturation under sustained upward or forward camera motion).

key_results.text: Matrix-Game 2.0 (Skywork, August 2025) streams 352x640 video at 25 fps on one H100 with about 1.8B parameters trained on about 1,200 hours of Unreal Engine, GTA driving, Minecraft, and Temple Run data, and releases weights and code; it has no explicit memory.

Hunyuan-GameCraft trained on over 1M recordings from more than 100 AAA titles; distillation raised speed from 0.25 to 6.6 fps with under 5 seconds latency per action, and weights released in August 2025 need at least 24 GB of GPU memory (80 GB recommended).

Yan (Tencent, August 2025) reports 1080p at 50 to 60 fps for its simulation module trained on the game Yuan Meng Star and an editing module that separates interactive mechanics simulation from visual rendering so text can restyle the world during play.

Matrix-Game 3.0 (April 2026) reaches up to 40 fps at 720p with a 5B model on an 8+1 GPU setup and keeps minute-long consistency by retrieving memory frames by camera pose; WorldPlay (Tencent Hunyuan) streams 720p at 24 fps with a reconstituted context memory for long-term geometric consistency.

Mirage 2 (Dynamics Lab, August 2025) lets players turn photos or sketches into browser-playable worlds and change them by typing commands, with saved and shared worlds, but struggles with precise controls and visual stability; Odyssey-2 (October 2025) generates each frame in under 50 ms from text prompts.

limitations: Resolution and speed trade against hardware: Matrix-Game 2.0 is 352x640 on one H100, Matrix-Game 3.0's 720p 40 fps needs 9 GPUs, and GameCraft runs at 6.6 fps after distillation.
Consistency horizon is about a minute even with retrieval memory; earlier open models have no explicit memory at all.
Training data includes recordings of commercial games (GTA V, 100+ AAA titles), so output provenance is contested.
Stronger history conditioning improves consistency but reduces responsiveness to new actions (GameCraft ablation).
Action spaces cover camera movement and basic locomotion; game verbs such as shooting, building, or trading are not modeled.
mechanism: A pretrained text- or image-to-video diffusion transformer (SkyReels-V2 for Matrix-Game 2.0, HunyuanVideo for GameCraft) gets action modules: keyboard and mouse mapped to camera translation and rotation, injected through cross-attention, token addition, or Plucker camera embeddings. Training uses gameplay recordings from Unreal Engine scenes, GTA V, Minecraft, Temple Run, or 100+ AAA titles. The bidirectional model is then distilled into a causal few-step generator (Self-Forcing with distribution matching, or phased consistency models) that streams chunks with a rolling KV cache. 2026 systems add memory by retrieving past frames whose camera pose overlaps the current view (Matrix-Game 3.0, WorldPlay). Yan, Mirage 2, and Odyssey-2 accept typed text during play to edit the world.
name: Open real-time interactive video world models
summary: Open and startup interactive video models (Matrix-Game, Hunyuan-GameCraft, WorldPlay, Yan, Mirage, Odyssey) adapt pretrained video diffusion transformers to keyboard and mouse control and stream frames in real time, adding pose-indexed memory and text edits during play.

affects.note: Cosmos is positioned for autonomous-vehicle training and closed-loop evaluation; a driving model post-trained from it predicts scene video under driving inputs with no tire or suspension model, which suits traffic scenarios more than the handling fidelity a racing sim needs.
Learned video dynamics could stand in for a physics engine in open-ended scenes, but near-chance IntPhys 2 scores show current models do not reliably reject impossible motion.
V-JEPA 2-AC scores candidate action sequences by predicted distance to a goal image in latent space, a learned alternative to hand-written utility curves for agents whose goals can be pictured.

key_results.text: Cosmos (January 2025) pretrained diffusion and autoregressive world foundation models on about 100M clips curated from about 20M hours of video and released them as open weights with permissive licenses.

Cosmos 3 ships Super 64B, Nano 16B, and Edge 4B models under the OpenMDW1.1 license, positioned for autonomous vehicle and robot synthetic data, closed-loop evaluation, and robot policy training, with no mention of games.
V-JEPA 2-AC, post-trained on under 62 hours of DROID robot video, performed zero-shot pick-and-place with image goals on Franka arms in two labs without task-specific data or reward.
On Meta's IntPhys 2 benchmark of physical plausibility, current video models including V-JEPA 2 score at or near chance while humans score 85 to 95 percent across the released benchmarks.

limitations: Designed for robots and vehicles; no game integration or game-specific evaluation exists in the cited sources.
Physical plausibility is unreliable: video models are at or near chance on IntPhys 2.
Large models (up to 64B in Cosmos 3) are far from per-player real-time budgets.
V-JEPA 2 predicts at a single time scale, limiting long-horizon planning (Meta's stated limitation).
mechanism: Cosmos curates about 20M hours of raw video into about 100M clips, compresses them with causal video tokenizers, and pretrains diffusion (Text2World, Video2World) and autoregressive world models that developers post-train into action- or camera-conditioned simulators; Cosmos 3 (2026) is an omni family at 4B, 16B, and 64B parameters. V-JEPA 2 instead predicts masked video in a learned embedding space, not pixels, from over 1M hours of video; its action-conditioned variant V-JEPA 2-AC is post-trained on under 62 hours of robot video and plans by searching for action sequences whose predicted embedding approaches a goal image.
name: Physical-world foundation models
summary: Video-pretrained models of physical dynamics, NVIDIA Cosmos for generating action-conditioned training video and Meta's V-JEPA 2 for latent prediction and planning, target robotics and driving rather than games.

affects.note: When an object advertises an interaction (sit, lie, lean), a goal-conditioned controller can perform it on new furniture geometry without a bespoke animation per object, as MaskedMimic shows for chairs, stools, and sofas.
The controlled character becomes a physical body that adapts footing to terrain and reacts to pushes, instead of playing canned clips that slide over geometry.
Characters join the rigid-body simulation as actuated bodies, so carried, pushed, and collided objects affect them and vice versa (InterMimic human-object interaction).

With a simulated body, a wound could change gait by limiting joint torque instead of swapping in an authored limp; the cited work does not demonstrate injury-conditioned motion, so this remains a projection.

key_results.text: MaskedMimic (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) formulates physics-based control as motion inpainting: one controller generates motion from keyframes, text, VR head or hand tracking, paths, or objects, and interacts with chairs, stools, tables, and sofas while transferring to irregular terrain; code is released as ProtoMotions.

InterMimic (2025) trains a single policy for physics-based human-object interaction from hours of imperfect motion capture by distilling subject-specific teacher policies and refining with RL; the authors report zero-shot generalization and compatibility with kinematic motion generators.

limitations: Every character needs a physics simulation step plus policy inference, which is costly at the hundreds-of-agents scale colony and management sims use; no crowd-scale runtime figures are published in the cited work.
Training requires large mocap datasets and GPU-parallel RL; retargeting to non-human or stylized rigs requires retraining.
Physical controllers can fall or jitter in edge cases, which is hard to QA across open-ended situations.
mechanism: A ragdoll with joint actuators is simulated in a physics engine; a policy network outputs PD targets each step and is trained with RL in massively parallel GPU simulation to track motion capture clips. MaskedMimic first trains a full-body tracker, then distills it into a conditional generative student that receives a masked goal: any subset of future joint positions, a text description, a head and hand signal from VR, a path, or a target object. The same controller therefore handles locomotion, steering, and sitting on varied furniture and transfers flat-ground motions to rough terrain. InterMimic distills per-subject teachers into one student refined by RL for whole-body human-object interaction from imperfect mocap.
name: Learned physics-based character control
summary: Neural policies trained with reinforcement learning drive simulated humanoids by joint torques to imitate motion capture, and MaskedMimic-style controllers accept partial goals such as keyframes, text, or an object to sit on.

affects.note: Mapping the build space by behavior descriptors, as was done for Hearthstone decks, shows the best design in each style niche, exposing dominant part combinations and empty niches before players find them.
Searching for the top-scoring design in every descriptor cell stress-tests the rating formula and surfaces degenerate designs that score well, such as rides or bridges that game the metric.

Instead of one seed-to-map generator, a game can ship an archive of maps spanning designer axes, such as resource density by chokepoint count, each verified by simulation and served to players by trait.
An archive of competitor strategies, each the strongest found for its niche (aggressive expander, low-price discounter), gives AI rivals distinct styles without hand-tuning each persona.
Scenario maps and starting conditions can be generated across a difficulty-by-style grid and filtered by agent playthroughs, replacing hand-built scenario sets with a curated archive.
Searches over module and beacon layouts expose dominant boosting configurations that collapse design choice.

key_results.text: MAP-Elites (2015) returns a map of high-performing solutions across user-chosen dimensions of variation, revealing trade-offs and often finding a better best solution than standard search.
Gravina et al. (IEEE CoG 2019) framed procedural content generation as a quality-diversity problem and reviewed early applications to content generation and game playing.
MAP-Elites with sliding boundaries mapped Hearthstone deck spaces along play-style dimensions, found diverse strong decks, and was proposed as an aid to rebalancing.

CMA-ME searching a GAN's latent space produced playable Super Mario Bros levels spanning designer-chosen measures such as enemy and obstacle counts, and a user study found those measures changed perceived difficulty.
DSAGE (2022) used a deep surrogate to predict agent behavior in generated environments and beat earlier QD environment-generation methods at finding environments that elicit diverse agent behaviors.

QDAIF (2023) used language models to generate variations and to judge quality and diversity of creative text, covering more of the target space than non-QD baselines with reasonable agreement with human raters.

limitations: Every candidate needs a fitness and descriptor evaluation, usually a simulated playthrough, so large archives cost many simulations; surrogate methods such as DSAGE exist to cut that cost.
Results depend on the chosen descriptors: poor choices give diversity along axes players do not perceive, and the grid grows exponentially with the number of descriptors.
Fitness measured with AI agents reflects agent skill, not human experience, so cells marked playable or balanced may not match player perception.
Game applications in the cited work are research prototypes on small games (Mario levels, Hearthstone decks); no documented shipped use in a simulation game was found in this run.
mechanism: The designer picks k behavior descriptors (for a level: enemy count and number of jumps; for a deck: mean mana cost and minion count) and discretizes them into a grid. Each cell stores the highest-fitness solution seen with those descriptor values. Each iteration selects elites from the archive, mutates or recombines them, evaluates the child's fitness and descriptors (usually by simulation or an agent playthrough), and inserts it if its cell is empty or it beats the incumbent. The archive shows which trait combinations can be good and how good. Variants slide cell boundaries to follow where solutions cluster (MESB), search a generative model's latent space with CMA-ES emitters (CMA-ME on a Mario GAN), use a learned surrogate to predict agent behavior and skip simulations (DSAGE), or use language models both to propose variations and to judge quality and diversity (QDAIF). GAVEL applies MAP-Elites to game rule sets.
name: Quality-diversity search (MAP-Elites) for content and balance
summary: Evolutionary search that keeps the best solution found in each cell of a grid of designer-chosen behavior descriptors, returning an archive of diverse high-quality levels, decks, or strategies instead of one optimum.

affects.note: Blocky player builds are rendered as detailed structures in a prompted style (for example Roman), a visual-only form of build assist: collision and block state stay coarse while the view is detailed.
Players or in-world logic change the whole world's look at runtime by text, without new textures or models; the game's systems cannot read the new look, so it carries no gameplay meaning.

key_results.text: MirageLSD responds in under 40 ms per frame at 24 fps, conditioning each frame on recent output, the current input frame, and a prompt; Decart lists limited memory, weak control of specific objects or regions, and structure distortion under extreme style shifts.
Oasis 2.0 is a Minecraft 1.21.8 mod that restyles the player's world in real time from prompts set by chat command or by in-world command blocks.

limitations: Short frame window and no long-term memory, so restyled objects can change appearance between views.
Rendered detail can contradict game state (a block that looks like a door but is solid), hurting legibility.
Cloud-served stream adds network latency and per-player GPU cost; no price per hour is published.
mechanism: The host game renders normally and streams its frames to a video-to-video diffusion model. Each output frame is conditioned on the current input frame, a window of recently generated frames, and a text prompt; Diffusion Forcing and history augmentation keep the stream from drifting, and distillation, pruning, and custom GPU kernels bring response under 40 ms at 24 fps. Because the model only replaces pixels, collision, inventory, and world state stay in the host engine. Decart's Oasis 2.0 packages this as a Minecraft mod with chat commands and command-block hooks that switch the prompt.
name: Real-time generative restyling of game video
summary: A live video-to-video diffusion model repaints each frame of a running game from a text prompt in under 40 ms, leaving the game's own simulation and state untouched.

affects.note: Characters can hold spoken, interruptible, full-duplex conversations with response onset near human turn-taking, replacing dialogue wheels or typed input; Whispers from the Star is built around this loop.
Delivery carries social meaning (whispering, sighing, hesitation, warmth) generated from conversational context, so the same line can land as a flirt, apology, or threat.
Squad orders can be spoken mid-action and parsed into function calls, as in PUBG Ally's voice-directed teammate, without menus.
Generated characters can get distinct designed or cloned voices and speak unscripted lines without recording sessions, which removes the voice-acting cost that keeps procedural characters silent.

claims.text: Eleven v3's expressive model was not recommended for real-time conversation at launch because of latency and reliability, so expressive range and low latency were still traded off in mid-2025.

A vendor case study reports Death by AI reached 20 million players in three months with 1.2 billion tokens in its first month after moving LLM and TTS to a gaming-priced provider; the cost claims are unverified.
Inworld's June 2026 price list puts streaming TTS at about $5-25 per million characters and speech-to-text at about $0.10 per hour, and claims only about 3 in 100 consumer AI users ever pay.

In GDC's 2026 survey of over 2,300 professionals, 36% used generative AI at work but 52% thought it was harming the industry, up from 30% in 2025, with game design and narrative (63%) and art (64%) among the most negative groups, which bears on adoption of generated character voices and dialogue.

key_results.text: Moshi reported 160 ms theoretical and 200 ms practical latency for full-duplex spoken dialogue.

OpenAI's Realtime API launched in October 2024 at about $0.06 per minute of audio input and $0.24 per minute of output; gpt-realtime (August 2025) priced audio at $32 and $64 per million input and output tokens and raised function-calling accuracy on ComplexFuncBench from 49.7% to 66.5%.
Sesame's CSM reached parity with human recordings in listener preference without conversational context, but listeners preferred the human recordings when 90 seconds of prior context was provided.
Inworld's TTS-1.5 (January 2026) lists P90 time to first audio under 130 ms (Mini) and under 250 ms (Max) at $15 and $25 per million characters, about $0.015-0.025 per minute of speech.

Whispers from the Star (August 2025) is built around open-ended voice, video-call, and text conversation with an AI-voiced character created with an actor, and Where Winds Meet (global November 2025) discloses real-time AI NPC text and voice chat.

ARC Raiders (November 2025) was criticized and marked down by Eurogamer for generative AI NPC voices, and the SAG-AFTRA video game strike (July 2024 to July 2025) ended with contract terms on consent for AI voice replicas.

limitations: Cost scales with talk time: at 2024 Realtime API rates, an hour split evenly between player and NPC speech is roughly $9 before context re-reads; gpt-realtime rates cut that to roughly $3 (estimates derived from list prices).
Expressive delivery and low latency trade off: context-conditioned prosody still trails humans, and the most expressive TTS was not suited to real time at launch.
Voice actor consent and compensation are now contract terms, and players have penalized AI voices in reviews.
Speech-native models are hard to constrain to game-legal actions; most games keep a text layer between speech and game state.
Microphone use and online connectivity raise privacy and access barriers (Whispers from the Star lists a broadband connection and an account).
mechanism: Two pipelines. Cascaded: streaming speech recognition, then an LLM, then streaming TTS, each optimized for time to first output. Speech-native: the model reads and writes audio tokens from a neural codec. Moshi models the user's and its own speech as parallel streams (full duplex, so it can listen while speaking) and predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens. Hosted realtime APIs keep a persistent WebSocket session with voice activity detection, interruption handling, and function calls that can trigger game actions. Expressive TTS conditions delivery on context: Sesame's CSM feeds prior conversation audio and text to a Llama-style backbone over codec tokens, and Eleven v3 accepts inline tags such as [whispers] or [sighs]. Small ASR and TTS models (hundreds of millions of parameters) can run on device.
name: Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters
summary: Streaming speech recognition, speech-native language models, and context-aware text-to-speech that let characters hold spoken, interruptible conversations with roughly 200-250 ms response onset and generated emotional delivery.

affects.note: The world is reconstructed from real imagery instead of generated from a seed and noise; the player-facing role of an explorable map is unchanged, but its content is the real planet, with procedural filling only where imagery is missing.

Recognizable real buildings and landmarks across the planet make visual navigation by reference to the ground practicable anywhere, extending hand-flying practice beyond hand-modeled airports and cities.
Learned classification of satellite imagery turns real-world map data into simulated scenery at planetary scale (Microsoft Flight Simulator).

key_results.text: Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) used Blackshark.ai's AI on Azure to generate 3D buildings, trees, and terrain from Bing Maps data and photogrammetry, covering about 1.5 billion buildings and 2 trillion trees from over two petabytes of streamed map data.
Blackshark.ai describes its products as turning satellite and aerial imagery into structured models of terrain, buildings, and infrastructure.
Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 carries over the satellite-derived scenery systems of the 2020 game.

limitations: Accuracy is bounded by imagery quality; blurred or pixelated areas fall back to procedural fill.
Requires cloud streaming of petabyte-scale data and a licensed imagery source.
Reconstructed buildings are generic from inferred class and height, not modeled individually, except in photogrammetry cities.
mechanism: Models trained on labeled imagery detect buildings, trees, and land cover in satellite and aerial imagery and map data and extrapolate approximate geometry; offline procedural generation then builds and dresses the buildings and places vegetation, while selected cities use photogrammetry meshes. The reconstruction runs offline in the cloud, and the result is streamed to players on demand as they fly, with procedural filling where imagery is poor.
name: ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery
summary: Machine learning classifies buildings, vegetation, and terrain in satellite and aerial imagery and procedural rules rebuild them as 3D scenery, which Microsoft Flight Simulator streams for the whole Earth.

affects.note: Transmission, recovery and contact parameters can be inferred from real outbreak curves or target curves, with a posterior that shows which parameters the data cannot pin down.
Economic ABM parameters can be calibrated to price and quantity time series (Dyer et al.), grounding market sims in real data instead of hand-set elasticities.
Demand and route-choice parameters of an agent-based traffic model can be fitted to observed counts, the same likelihood-free ABM calibration applied to a city.
Match-engine parameters can be fitted so simulated score and statistic distributions match real league data, with uncertainty on each parameter.
Predator-prey rates can be inferred from target population time series, so designers state desired oscillations and the posterior returns rates that produce them.
Treating target survival-time or loss-rate distributions from playtest telemetry as the observation, the posterior gives scaling parameters that reproduce them and how sensitive each one is.

key_results.text: Cranmer, Brehmer and Louppe reviewed simulation-based inference as a general framework for inverse problems in simulators with intractable likelihoods.

Automatic posterior transformation (APT) made sequential neural posterior estimation work with arbitrary, dynamically updated proposals and flow-based estimators, including on high-dimensional time series and images.

Neural posterior and neural ratio estimation gave state-of-the-art parameter inference for economic agent-based models from multivariate time series, where older likelihood-free methods needed hundreds of thousands of simulations.
Temporal graph neural networks learned ABM parameter posteriors directly from microdata, avoiding information loss from hand-chosen summary statistics.
The open-source sbi toolkit packages these estimators with diagnostics and defaults, needing only simulator samples.

limitations: Needs many simulator runs, from thousands to hundreds of thousands depending on method and dimensionality, which is costly for slow, full-scale game simulations.
A misspecified simulator yields confident posteriors over wrong parameters; calibration fits the data and does not validate the model.
Posterior quality depends on the summary statistics or learned embeddings of noisy, high-dimensional outputs.
Matching real data or telemetry targets does not make a mechanic fun; it only removes guesswork about parameter values.
No game studio use was found in this run's sources.
mechanism: Draw parameters theta from a prior, run the simulator to get outputs x, and train a conditional density estimator, usually a normalizing flow, to approximate p(theta | x) from the (theta, x) pairs (neural posterior estimation). Conditioning on observed data x_o gives the posterior; sequential variants such as APT draw new simulations from proposals concentrated near x_o. Related variants learn the likelihood or a likelihood ratio instead. Summary statistics can be hand-chosen or learned, for example with a temporal graph neural network over agent-level microstates. The method needs only forward runs, no likelihood and no gradients, and once trained it is amortized: a new observation gets its posterior in one forward pass.
name: Simulation-based inference for calibrating simulators
summary: Neural density estimators trained on simulator runs return a posterior over a simulator's parameters given observed data, calibrating agent-based and economic models whose likelihoods cannot be computed.

affects.note: Deformation learned from an offline solver runs 300-5000x faster than that solver, putting near-offline-quality cloth and flesh response within a real-time budget.
Hands-on tasks such as surgery or handling soft objects could show tissue and cloth reacting plausibly to tools in real time, adding feedback the player reads to perform the skill.

key_results.text: Ubisoft La Forge's subspace neural physics ran interactive cloth and deformable simulation 300 to 5000 times faster than conventional simulation at a small additional memory cost (the project page states 300 to 4000).

Unreal Engine's ML Deformer trains models on externally generated deformation caches from Maya or Houdini and applies them at runtime as GPU morph targets; the Neural Morph Model is the recommended default and the cloth-oriented Nearest Neighbor Model is marked experimental.

limitations: Quality holds only near the training distribution of poses and interactions; unusual poses or collisions produce artifacts, so coverage of the offline dataset sets the limit.
Training is heavy: Unreal's documentation notes long training times and Alembic training caches of 50-100 GB.
GPU memory for morph targets is the main runtime cost, and compression settings trade memory and speed for quality.
Output is usually cosmetic; it does not feed back into gameplay physics unless the game reads the deformed state, which brings determinism and consistency issues.
No commercial title using these models at runtime was confirmed in this run's sources.
mechanism: Developers run an expensive offline simulation (cloth, soft tissue, muscle, volume-preserving flesh) over many randomized poses or interactions. Vertex positions are compressed, for example with principal component analysis, into a low-dimensional subspace. A small network is trained to predict the next subspace coordinates from the current coordinates plus external inputs such as bone transforms or collider positions (Holden et al. 2019), or to predict per-pose corrective morph-target weights applied on top of linear skinning (Unreal Engine ML Deformer, Neural Morph Model and Nearest Neighbor Model). At runtime only the network and the decode from subspace to full mesh run, on the GPU.
name: Subspace neural physics and learned deformers
summary: Small networks trained on offline cloth, flesh, or muscle simulation predict deformation in a compressed subspace or as corrective morph targets, running hundreds to thousands of times faster than the source simulation inside a game engine.

affects.note: Decor and furniture catalogs that beauty and environment scores consume can be produced from prompts or reference images in seconds per asset, so catalog size stops being bounded by modeling time.
Runtime generation extends from text and textures to placeable 3D props: inZOI players convert their own images into in-game objects.

Part-controllable generation (Roblox CubePart) produces assets split into parts intended for physics and scripts, which could supply new components for build-from-parts mechanics on request; not yet shown in a shipped assembly game.

key_results.text: TRELLIS (Microsoft, CVPR 2025) trains models up to 2B parameters on about 500K 3D objects and decodes one latent to radiance fields, 3D Gaussians, or meshes; it is MIT-licensed and needs a GPU with at least 16 GB.
TRELLIS.2 (4B parameters) outputs PBR-textured GLB assets in about 3 seconds at 512^3, 17 seconds at 1024^3, and 60 seconds at 1536^3 on an H100.
Hunyuan3D 2.0 (January 2025) released open shape and texture models; Hunyuan3D 2.1 (June 2025) added PBR texturing and training code and needs about 29 GB of VRAM for shape plus texture.
Roblox released Cube 3D text-to-shape (v0.1 March 2025, v0.5 July 2025) and CubePart part-controllable generation (May 2026) aimed at assets usable with animation, physics, and scripts.
inZOI's store page states that players can turn 2D images into in-game 3D objects, with AI tools described as auxiliary and generated content reviewed by the team.
inZOI received negative user reviews in May 2025 after Krafton announced its use of generative AI.

limitations: Hardware: 16 GB (TRELLIS) to about 29 GB (Hunyuan3D 2.1 shape plus texture) of GPU memory, so player-side generation usually runs in the cloud or on high-end PCs.
Output topology and UVs are not authored for animation or LOD; production use still needs cleanup and review, which inZOI states it applies.
Generated assets are single objects without gameplay semantics; the game must assign function, footprint, and value.
Training data provenance and licenses vary by model, and player reception of generative AI can be negative (inZOI reviews in 2025).
mechanism: Generation is split into shape and appearance. A flow-matching or diffusion transformer generates a 3D latent conditioned on an image or text: TRELLIS uses a Structured LATent (sparse voxels carrying features from a vision foundation model), Hunyuan3D-DiT a shape latent, and Roblox Cube discrete shape tokens predicted autoregressively. Decoders turn the latent into meshes, 3D Gaussians, or radiance fields. Texture is painted by a multi-view diffusion model (Hunyuan3D-Paint) or decoded directly, with 2025 versions emitting PBR maps (base color, roughness, metallic). Output is a GLB or OBJ file that drops into an engine like any other asset.
name: Text- and image-to-3D asset generation
summary: Open 3D generative models (TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D 2.x, Roblox Cube) produce textured meshes from a text prompt or image in seconds to a minute, and inZOI exposes image-to-3D object creation to players.

affects.note: The player can describe a behavior in language and the model writes, tests against the live game, and saves the program, so player code becomes a growing library of named skills rather than hand-typed scripts.
An NPC's competence can be an accumulating library of composable, verified routines it wrote itself, so skill growth adds new behaviors rather than raising a numeric speed or quality level.
A delegated controller can acquire routines for situations its designers did not code by writing and verifying new functions, instead of running the fixed opponent-AI logic restricted to a subsystem.
Exploration agents that unlock milestones 15.3x faster than earlier agents can be run as automated playtesters to measure how quickly and in what order a progression graph gets traversed.
Demonstrated routines can be stored as verified, reusable code skills that generalize to new locations.

key_results.text: Against prior LLM agents, Voyager obtained 3.3x more unique items, traveled 2.3x longer distances, and unlocked tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster, discovering 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations.
The learned skill library let a fresh agent solve novel tasks in a new Minecraft world from scratch, where baselines struggled.
Code generation quality was the bottleneck: replacing GPT-4 with GPT-3.5 for code produced 5.7x fewer unique items, while GPT-4 cost 15x more per token.

In the 2025 Factorio Learning Environment, LLM agents writing code found growth strategies such as electric drilling but failed at complex automation such as electronic-circuit production, with weak spatial reasoning and error recovery.

limitations: Depends on a frontier code model; GPT-3.5 produced 5.7x fewer items and GPT-4 cost 15x more per token, so per-agent cost is high.
Hallucinated tasks and calls: the curriculum proposed items that do not exist (copper sword), and generated code used invalid inputs or functions absent from the API, causing execution errors.
Self-verification misjudges success (for example not recognizing a dropped string as proof a spider was defeated).
Needs a scripting API that exposes game actions and state as text; it does not act from pixels.
Long-horizon factory building in Factorio still fails at multi-step automation and spatial layout.
mechanism: Voyager drives a Minecraft bot through a JavaScript control API.
